" YES," he said," before marriage I thought I could live on love. But I am now living en my father-in-law." "I WOULDN'T be a fool, if I were you," said Jones to a friend. "If yau were I, you wouldn't be a fool," was the reply. ~„,. IT has been suggested that one reason why the communications of spirits are so indistinct is because they write on rapping" paper. "I'LL be wiser when I'm moulder," as the moialder's appreutice remarked to his employer when chidden for some mistake he had made. "LOOKING at your drawing imbues me with an artistic fever," remarked Smith to Miss Lulu. "I thought -so; it's sketching," quietly replied Miss Lulu. "Yon have no idea," said the landlord, "how much it costs to run tills hotel." " Oh, yes, 1 have," replied the guest; "I paid up my bill this , morning." Tux man who robs a clothes-line is not , necessarily a lanndr2,:man, bizt he generally "takes in" washing, and is likely to be ironed if he is , can alit. Ctarriata.—At a ball a girl said to her part- ner who was a very poor ancer : "Do you like waltzing?" "I adore it," he repiied. "Then why did you newer learn ?" she ihquired. A MAN said to his aged mother, speaking of his wife, "I do so with I could keep Mary from ex- aggerating so "Get her to talk about her own age," responded the shrewd Li lady. AT a college examination a professor asked " Does the question embarrass you ?" " Not at all," replied the student ; "not at all. The ques- tion is quite clear. It is the answer that bothers me." "Is anybody waiting on you ?" said a polite salesman to a young lady from the country. "Yes, sir," replied the blushing damsel. "That's my youog man outside; he wouldn't come into the shop." • SCENE—country house; time after dinner. Old friend —" You ought to be proud of your wife, Joe." liost—"Yes." Oiti jrie74d—" She's a most brilliant talker." host--" Sue ought to be." Old friend—" I could listen to her for a wliole night." hoot (wearil) )—" I often do I" ACCEPTING HIS APOLOGY.—" I have never given you credit for knowing very much, madam," said a blunt old bachelor • " but—" "Sir," she interrupted, "do you wish to insult—" "But," he continued, "I have always admired your grace and beauty." "I accept your apology,' said the

lady. "AND don't you know, Johnny," said the minister, who was dining with the family, "why your mamma doesn't want you to eat a second piece of pie?" "Yes, sir," replied Johnny. "She said that if I didn't eat a second piece, and you didn't take any, there would be enough left over for to-morrow." Senoor. TEXT-WORS give " milk " as a perfect example of a food which contains all the essential ingredients of a mixed diet. The example of a mixed diet once given by a boy at a written examination was "a sausage." The example given by a girl at the same examination was "roast duck, potatoes, and green peas, and a little jam tart afterwards." MERE was a feud between the four-year-old young lady and her aunt, which came at last to declared hostilities. But the little lady knelt down at night and said her prayers—" Bless papa, and bless mamma, and "—there came a long, ominous pause—" bless auntie; but if you can't bless her it doesn't matter."

AWFUL LONESOHE.—A Ettle fellow five or six years old, who had been wearing flannel jackets much too small for him, was one day, after being watched, put into a garment as much too large as the other hail been too small. Our six- year-old shrugged his shoulders, shook himself, walked about, and finally burst out: "Ma, I do feel awful lonesome in this jacket I" "PRISONER," said a Nevada judge, "What have you to say to this indictment; are you guilty or not guilty ?" "Before I answer the question, judge, I'd like to ask your honour if this little spec- tacled dude is all the lawyer I've got ?" "That is I.lr. Ferguson, sir," responded the judge, sternly ; "I have appointed him to defend you, as you seem to have no counsel." "Judge," said the prisoaer, sighing heavily, " I am guilty." CHARLES had beeu courting Cara for six months without coming to the point, when she turned on him one evening with : " Utirles, isn't it awful for a girl like me to have to worry over how I shall invest 475,000 ?" He thought it was, and three months later they were !named. "I'll invest that $75,000 for you, my dear," he observed, a day or two after marriaga. 'oh ! I was afraid some one might love me for my money, and I gave it to papa," was the artless reply. A WEAVER from Elderslie happening lately to be public-house in Johnstwae, an English trades- man was pnrent, who was boasting to another peraon that he had got quit of his wife by selling her at Smithfield, and seemed happy at the good bargain he had made. The weaver, tickled with the recital, was curious enough to al the price he had received for his wife. " Well, frien ,' an' how rnuckle might ye get for her, gif it be a fair question?" ." A pot of beer !" " Hech man ! she has been unco little worth, or ye hae been very dry at the time." A RtSPFCTABLE farmer in the parish of Cum- nook, being a widower, went a-courting a young lady, the daughter of a neighbouring farmer in the pariah of Auchinleck. The farmer, who was no great orator, but was young, had a good person, and was in affluent circumstances, addressed his fair one rather bluntly, and proposed marriage without much ceremony. The any replied, in the same frank and open way, '',Dced J in.ie, I'll tak ye, but ye mann gie me my dues 0' i.ourtin' for a' that." The wedding took place accordingly. IT was when dining with a friend in Worcester College (says Miss Whately) that a trifling inci- dent brought out one of Whately'e happiest bona mote. There were some medlars on the table, and his host regretted that he had in vain tried to pro- cure also some services ( Pyrus Domesticas), a fruit 'which grows wild in Kent and Sussex, and is there called chequers." One of the company asked the -difference betwLen a " service " and a • meddler," tolvtlich Whately replied, "The same kind of 'llifference as between offieium' and officisous.' " A LIVERPOOL lady called at a police station the other day and complained to a superintendent that her husband had, in the most cruel manner, kept her a prisoner at home for the last ten days. " Ah," said the superintendent, "does he lock the doors on you?" "Certainly not." "Does he have somebody to guard you and kec you from going out?" No, indeed; not he I" "Well, does he—does he t-t-tie you to anything?" "No, sir; ho dare not," "Well, I should say, madam, that—pray excuse me—that you have about all the freedom you could want." "Gracious heavens l" exclaimed the lady, with clenched fingers and flashing eyes, "a horrid mouse tied to the top of the box with my Sunday bonnet in it; and you talk to me about all the freedom I could want I" A DISTINGUISHED actor, calling at the house of a lady, was, while the mother was getting ready, received by the daughter, aged twelve. The dis- tinguished actor thought he was right in suiting his conversation to his juvenile company. When he had gone the damsel expressed a very poor opinion of his small talk. But," it was explained, "he thinks you are a nice little girl, and speaks to you as he would to other little girls." "Well, all I can say," replied the child, "he's just the same silly old fool when he's taking to mamma." A COUNTRY COUSIN, who had come up en garcon '4 'just for the Jubilee, had somewhat outstayed his welcome at the house of a London friend, and, as ho showed no symptoms of departing, his host a miming or two ago said to him—" Well, I don't (2c.'vd#h to hurry you, old fellow, hut don't you think is time you saw your wife and children again, eh? Why, they will be growing inconsolable for the . loss of you?' HONOUR.

The nearest way to honour is for a man so to five that he might be found to be that in truth he would be thought to be. 'Tis honourable to support the glory of one's ancestors, by actions which correspond with their reputation; and it is also glorious to leave a title to one's descendants which is not borrowed from our predecessors; to become the head and author of our own nobility; and (to use the expression of Tiberius, who was desirous of hiding the defect of birth in Curtius Rufus, though otherwise a very great man) to be born of one's own self. True honour is seated in the soul. It rises from a generous heart, and flows with a natural and easy descent into all the different traces of life and channels of duty, refreshing, invigorating, and adorning all the faculties of the soul, the language of the tongue, the very air of the face, and motions of the Cody. It displays itself in a natural unaffected greatness and firmness of mind, improved by a train of wise and religious reflections and generous actions, in which personal virtue and real merit truly consist. The Jewish Cabalists had a pretty allegory to express this truth, as founded in the original make and frame of nature. They tell us, that, when Moses describes the great river of Eden branching out into four streams, we are to understand by paradise the mind or soul of man. The river was this original fountain of truth and virtue, arising from the very root and essence of the soul, and branching out into the four cardinal virtues, and all the other lower degrees and kinds of virtue— even the inferior morals of affability,politeness, good nature, and good manners; and that, in short, there lies hid in the root of every human soul, however defaced by ignorance and deformed by vice, a fund of good, an oracle of truth, which, when assisted by a happy concurrence of external causes—such as, particularly, the structure of the organs and the tex- ture of the blood and spirits—will, by due culture and discipline, naturally exert itself into a train of great, generous, and beneficent actions suitable to the origi- nal grandeur and dignity of its nature. This, in the present debased state of human nature, lies very often buried under the ruins of ignorance and vice, like valuable coins, medals, statues, pillars, and other beau- tiful ornaments of architecture—or, to speak more properly, that order, symmetry, and proportion, which were as the soul of the structure—lie buried under he ruins of a once famous and magnificent building. nce it comes to pass,that many an excellent genius s lost, to the world—lies hid amongst the rubbish of nkind—who, with proper assistance, due culture, d in a happy situation, might have done honour to ,i man nature, and been a public blessing to mankind. A man of honour, considered in this light, performs not only all the acts of virtue in public and private life, but does them with a peculiar propriety and dig- nity of behaviour, as the connoisseurs in writing, painting, music, architecture, or even dress, execute , even the justest 4esigns, not only with proportion and truth, but with such decorations, embellishments, and graces, as naturally flow from a fine taste and an improved understanding. This alone, in high life, makes glorious princes, illustrious heroes, gallant commanders, vigilant magistrates, and honourable counsellors; and, in the lower degree of social life, indulgent husbands, tender fathers, affectionate friends, merciful landlords and masters, faithful tenants and servants; and executes all the relative duties of life with justice and honour. This is the true and real virtue, the only proper foundation of all the honourable distinctions among men in all the different stations of life. The bulk of mankind are caught by noise and show . The pompous sound of titles and glitter of ornaments strike their senses, attract their attention, raise their ad- miration, and extort from them all that re- verence and regard which are due only to eminent and distinguished merit ; while real virtue and true honour pass eileutly through the world, unheeded and unregarded but by the happy discernieg few who are sens'.ble of its merit, or en: joy the blessed communication of its influence. When those glorious spirits, whom Providence has appointed to be our guardians and protectors in this present state of imperfection and probation, survey the Cdsordered state of human nature, agitated by blind passions, prejudiced by false opinions, into erroneous conclusions and wild pursuits, they view us with the same light, and with the same emotions of compassion and charity, as Monroe did his lunatic patients in Bedlam, who miseal and misapply almost every instance In which their duty and happiness is concerned. 'To those blessed intelligences, the silent life a a generous, compassionate, beneficent man, is more truly honourable than the pageantry of princes, tlas pomp of conquerors, and all the glorious impertine ence of state. To them, an obscrire good man, doing: secret acts of charity, relieving the distressed, com- forting the miserable, and approving himself, by habits of piety and devotion, to the great Author of his being, appears more truly glorioni than the con- querer at the head of a hundred thousand men. To them the Man of I:ass appears in a fairer light in the Book of Remembrance; and will ever make a much more illustrious figure at the last great day, than Alexander, or Cmsar, or William the Conqueror, though, a Chris- tian. For to do, good, to be lovers of mankind, to alleviate the distresses, and promote the peace and happiness of our fellow-ereatnres, is the highest honour, the noblest ambition, that can enter into the heart of a man. But the greatest part at man- kind judge quite otherwise. Noise and show,, title and equipage, glitter and grandeur, constitute the whole idea of honour; and whoever can command an interest sufficient to procure, and an affluence sufficient to support them, becomes thereby not only a man of honour, but even a subordinate Immo. tam n of honour to others.

THE amount of short hair scattered over car bodies is very variable. In the male it is always more plentiful than in the female, and certain race& such as the Ainos, the Australians, the Todos ot the Nilgherries, are distinguished for their hairiness while othels, such as the African Negroes and the Mongolians, show scarcely a trace of hair on, their bodies. Amongst the AMos, indeed, the hair over the shoulders and on the back and limbs is some- • times so thick and long as to deserve the name of fur.. IN personal behaviour carefully avoid the follow- ing things :—Loud and harsh speaking; making noises in eating and drinking; leaning awkwardly when sitting; starting up suddenly and going un- ceremoniously out of the room; taking anything without thanking the giver; standing in the way; going before anyone who is looking at anything; interrupting anyone who is conversing with you; telling long and tiresome stories; whispering in company; flatly contradicting anyone; using slang expressions; asking questions or alluding to subjects which may give pain; neglecting to answer letters.. THERE is nobody among us who, having worn himself out in toil, has not seen the hours of rest approach with supreme delight. Life for- some of os is only one long day of weariness, and death a long slumber, and the coffin a bed of rest, and the earth only a pillow, where it is sweet, when all is done, to lay one's head never to raise it again. I confess to you that, when looked at in this way, death is the most agreeable of prospects. I am bent on teaching myself more and more to see it so.—Diderot. THERE are in knowledge these two excellences— first, that it offers to every man, the most selfish and the most exalted, his peculiar inducement to good. It says to the former, "Serve mankind, and you serve yourself ;" to the latter, "In choosing the best means to secure your own happiness, you will have the sublime inducement of promoting the happiness of mankind." The second excellence of knowledge is that even the selfish man, when he has once begun to love virtue from little motives, loses the motive as he increases the love, and at last worships the Deity, where before he only coveted gold upon. its altar. THE wife of Thomas Goffe, the poet, was a nig- gardly woman. Once some of his Oxford friends paid a visit to him at East Clane.on, where be was rector. The wife looked upon them with an ill eye, and provided a dish of milk and some eggs for supper, and no more. They, perceiving her stingi- ness, and that her husband was put out at it (she wearing the breeches) resolved to have some fun at supper, so they all talked Latin and laughed a great deal. She was so vexed at their speaking Latin that she could not contain herself, began to cry, and left the table. The nextday Mr. (Joffe ordered a better dinner for them and sent for some wine, but his wife did not put in an appearance. Not long after this Mr. Goffe died, heart-broken, it was said, by his wife's hard, narrow, and disagreeable ways.

There is a curious piece of news by Monday's Australian mail. Mr. William Fox, one of • the wealthiest Irish citizens of Melbourne;bas intimated his intention of erecting, at a cost of £6,000, statues in Ireland—Glasnevin is his preference—to the memory of Mitchel, Meagher, and other Irish patriots of the past. s. Of the fifty-four cardinals now living, thirty-four are Italians; four are Austrians or Hungarians; six are French; two are Portuguese; one is a Beige; two are Americans; one is an Irishman; one is an Englishman; and three are 6paniards. Of those three are British subjects—Cardinal Howard now in Rome, Cardinal Moran in Australia, and Cardinal Tachereau in Quebec.

Trade is not improving yet. The Board of Trade returns for January shows decrease in expor- tations as compared with January,lB9l, of £657,000, and, an increase of importations of £4,744,000. This, on the face of it, is fairly satisfactory, but it must be remembered that January last year was a very bad month. The severe weather and the Scotch railway strike paralysed industry. The last month's record does not, therefore, carry us over the period of depression.

Mr. Victor Cavendish is no longer the youngest member of Parliament in point of years. That dis- tinction is due to Mr. William Danvers Smith, the son of the late Mr. W. H. Smith, who on Tuesday took his seat for the Strand Division. Mr. Caven- dish is heir presumptive to his uncle the Duke of Devonshire,while Mr. Smith is heir apparent to his mother, who was created Viscountess Hambleton. Mr. Cavendish was born on 31st May, 1868, and Mr. Smith on 12th August of the same year.

Mr. Chamberlain has been appointed "leader of the Liberal Unionist party in the House of Com- mons," and it would have been hard to find a more suitable man. He is the type of the Liberal Unionist. For all that we know of the Liberal is that he has turned from the paths of Liberalism, and all that we know of the Unionist is that he has disunited Unionism. Abjuring whet he formerly adored only to adore what he formerly abjured, he finds in the Tory the true Liberal and in the Liberal the faults he once saw in the Tory.

A short time ago the Italian Government refused permission to Cardinal Lavigerie to found a monas- tery for African monks at Cagliari. It saw in the monks, says our Paris Correspondent, disguised soldiers who in the event of a Franco-Italian quarrel might throw off their gowns and fight for France and the Pope. The Cardinal angered at this, has, he says, determined to imitate Hannibal by carrying the war into the heart of the enemy's country. He has therefore bought a large house and vineyard in the suburbs of Rome, near the Porta Latina. His monks are to cultivate the vineyard.

Justice Bradley, a member of the United States Supreme Court, who died recently, was one of the most striking illustrations of the possibilities of life in the republic across the sea. The son of apoor farmer, unable to secure in early life more than ten weeks each year at a little country school, he has just died a leading member of the highest court of his native land, a Court known and respected in every corner of the world. And although Mr. Bradley never reached the highest office in the gift of the American people, his casting vote in the con- tested election of 1876 placed Hayes in the Presi- dential chair. The protectionist party are early in evidence this session. The first amendment moved to the Queen's speech was one by Mr. J. Lowther and COL Howard Vincent in favour, not of " fair trade "'—that un- popular phrase has been superseded—but of "pre- ferential trading relations.' Sir M. Hicks-Beach threw told water on the absurd proposals, and Mr. Morley tripped up Mr. Lowther very neatly. The preferential trader was reminding the House that England had committed a gross injustice to Ireland years ago by the extinction of her manufacturing industries-, That was done by English protec- tionists," said Mr. Morley. Needless to say the preferential trading relations amendment was de- feated without a division.

-- Mr. John: Morley, on Saturday, at Newcastle, made some excellent criticisms on Mr. Chamberlain's proposed pension scheme. It comes to this, that Mr. Morley does not see how it will work. The ofi%r which it makes is that if a man at twenty-five years of age deposits .£5 in the savings bank, and goes on paying a sovereign a year for forty years, then when he b sixty-five the State.will guarantee that he gets ss. a week forthe rest of his life. As Mt Morley remarked, this-incentive to thrift is ratter a shadowy one, and his audience, consisting of members of the Loyal Order of Ancient Shep- herds, thoroughly agreed will "What,' Mr. Morley asked, "under this scheme was to become of the dockers, the hawkers, the men who live by casual labour, the, great host, of agricultural la- bourers ? How was-an agriculturallabourer on las. or 12s:.a week, and, with three or fbur children to maintain, going to put by £4s' before he reached the age of sixty-five ?"

Irun :Ma been mentioned several 'times as one of the places where Mrs, Osborne remained in conceal- ment while abroad. it is even less known to the public than Gisors, and owes its little reputation to the facv that it is a frontier -sillage where the tourist, ott his way from Bayonne to,Madrid, stops to change-carriages and to have hispassports vised. Here he may derive his.first impressions of Spanish life and scenery from the white-plastered houses with their- tiled and protruding roofs and their , marvellous, iron balconies, on which the women spend their days under striped canvas awning. 'Tb are is a magnificent view of the Pyrenees, sloping , away in harmonious undulation to, the sea, and backed by the gulf near which Bayonne and Biarritz stand sentinel. The whole, plus a prinaitive wagon, 1, whose creaking wheels emit a sound like" anumber ;of jays being plucked alive, of efildren being I whipped, °Nuts making 'Awe, and of saws scraping their teeth against a hard stone," hasbeen charm- ingly described by Theophile Gautier.

A _ VISIONS OF BOU BLESS WEALTH. (A scene from "had He Known," a story of the New Zealand Gold Thirst, just commenced in " Cassell's Family Magazine.") Beturning home, after the question of the land had been settled, Ingram went to work at his Mine with redoubled energy. Logan and Burnt were not likely to betray him, and, in truth, under the pies- ; L sure of other matters,had almost forgotten him and , his affairs. The secret was still locked up in the breast of the lonely man, who stealthily took the same way every morning, who worked till late in the day, and who at night could hardly sleep for thoughts of the riches that would shortly be his— the happier, brighter future abqut to dawn. Some- times, in broken slumbers, he dreamed of telling his wife, of spreading before her heaps of gold, and saying, "See, all these are yours ; and you shall never be poor or wearied or troubled any more. The best things the world can give are all for you, who gave up everything to share my sorrow and my want." Then he would awake, trembling and over- wrought with his extravagant joy. So far all had gone as he wished; he had not attracted any undue amount of attention. But at home there was one who watched him, and won- dered anxiously what might be the cause of his changed demeanour. So silent and reserved had he become that his children were afraid of him, his wife shrank from questioning him about his long absences. At first she had thought he must be clearing or fencing at the farther and of the farm, where this work was required. But while he laboured there other and more important things were neglected. He seemed to have abandoned his farm. When his wife timidly reminded him of bills unpaid, of work undone, he put her off with assur- ances that all would be right by and by ; she had only to wait a little longer. Wait! Poor enough they had always been, now starvation stared them in the face. Distracted by his extraordinary cos- duct, Mrs. Ingram hardly knew which way to turn. The whole matter was an inexplicable, heart-break- ing mystery. She seldom visited the settlement; she saw no one who could have told her of Ingram's search for gold. From himself no information was to be extracted. At night—the only time he was with his family—he sat as if absorbed in visions and in dreams, from which he had resolved not to awake, smiling vacantly or muttering to himself. At the rare times when he would talk freely, it was some extravagant rhapsody of better days that were coming to them all. "We'll be out of the chrysalis stage soon," he exclaimed. "We'll unfold our wings and fly! " " Ah I if we only could I° said Mrs. Ingram,with a weakly smile. "Where woul€l you fly to,Emily " said Ingram ; "say the word only. Shall it be home again? I'd like to see the old place, wouln't you, dear ? did not notice that his wife was silently crying— " and the old folks too, though they were a little hard with us. Shall it be Sydney and the Blue Mountains? or Melbourne and the Gippsland Lakes? or the round trip—through Australasia and the Pacific Islands? We've the world to choose from."

"I'm afraid our wings are sadly clogged," said Mrs. Ingram. " The clogs are easily got rid of. Isn't it de- lightful to think that as yet we've seen nothing, and that evelything will be fresh to us? All the wonderful things in great cities, all the splendid paintings and sculpture, all the grind music, all the beautiful sce.iery in all countries of the world ! Should we ever be tired of wondering,, ever wears of seeing, ever satisfied with hearing? " I don't know, dearest,' said his wife,. watching his eager face and glittering eyes, while a sudden, terrible fear chilled her to the heart. •

The next day Ingram determined to kw the result of his crushing. He was feeling strange that morning, dizzy and faint, as if his strength were exhausted, and considering the rate at which he had been living, this was highly probable.. Still upheld by strong excitement, he rode to the settle- ment, and presented himself at Logan's office in the Diadem Company's establishment. Here there was great bustle and activity ;Abe battery was at work, and twenty head of stamper& were descending with a frightful din, which, so far from irrigating the servants of the Company or injnring their nerves, was rather liked by them;; the manager averring that it had a soporific effect on him, and that if it stopped in the-night he imme- diately awoke. Eve.fyone* was busy, Logan eDeci- ally, and it was some time before he-could be seen. When at last Ingram was alone withthim,he fancied that he looked at him pityingly, and was in no haste to satisfy hisimpatience. "You will guess that I've come to ask about the crushing," said,lngram nervously. _ . .

It might be only-a fancy, but -he thought he read the signal of failure in Logan's face, and felt him- self turn white 4170-the very lips. "Can you bear o, disappointment ?" said Logan kindly. Ingram made no answer. "I am as much astonished as you C C. 71 be at that crushing. There was absolutly nothing in it like ,the samples. I hove your word for it that they were genuine, and I do not for a moment doubt it. I Still, I am obliged to tell you that you have spent your time and. Strength in excavating a barren "There was no gold in it ?" said Ingram faintly, "So little, that 1 might almost say none at all." There was a pause- It seemed to Ingram as if Logan hod receded into an immense black shadow, and that between this-and himself the furniture of the laboratory was whizzing round and round in a, furious maelstom. Ile himself was falling into the same, and sinking down, down into eternal dark- ness. Ilands touched him.. Logan was supporting him to a chair; an assistant ran out and returned with some brandy, which they gave him. He came to himself again, and sat up. "Don't let this upset yon," said Logan,. his arm still around him. "I am ashamed," he faltered. "I tzld you it was rife- or ckath to me."' " Tut ! tut !" saide Treloar, the maaager of the battery, a big-framed, good-hearted Cornishman, whobad hurried in to see what was amiss. "Never say die, man! Youfllive to laugh at this !" find your gold yet in the fields of your farm" Ingram scarcely heard him. "1 have to thank you, Mr. Logan," he said; "you've been exceedingly kind. I've only my own ignoranco to blame. I hope you or Mr. Treloar will tell me what I have to pay the company.. shouted Treloar ; " why,nothing at all. You brought the first grist to our mill, yours was the first load that went through our battery. Are we going to charge for that, do youNthink 2 Logan, are we vampires? "Not that aware of replied his coadjutor. " I assure you, Mr. Ingram, thsre'a nothing to said the broken man, looking bewilder- ingly from one to the other, "Good morning,gentle- men. I think"--and the smile on his face was 'piteous to beheld—" I'd better go kome.'.% 'WARRING-ON BOARD, OF GUARDIANS..

A small allowance was paid to him weekly fsr his services, and he hoped the Board would take into their consideration the question of providing him with ,extra remuneration.—Mr. Susanna stated that Mr. Wallace was receiving a guinea a week.—Mr. Alfred JOLLY moved that the salary be increased to 255. per week.—This was seconded by the Rev. We are now 1 paying Mr. Harbourne his full salary of £l6O a year.— The CLERK: In addition to the 255. a week paid to Mr. Wallace.—Mr. Ratcliffe contended that officers of the Union were well paid, and that they ought to• provide a superannuation fund for themselves when in good health. I—lt1—It was decided, after some further discussion, that a petition be presented to the Local Government Board requesting the promotion of a Bill in Parliament to regulate the amount of superannuation by proportional , reductions from officers' salaries, and an augmentation of the fund by the State.—Mr. DAVIES also gave notice , 'that he would bring forward a motion at the next meet- ing with reference to the superannuation of Mr. 1 Harbourne.

Yard, ; Thomas Carey, son of Michael Carey, 29,R055 and Crown-street, William Holiwell, 8011 of Bliss, bath Holiwell, 20, Littca's Row, Jblin William Spencer, son of William Spencer, 79, Mersey-street,. John Henry Holiwell, brother of William Holiwell,.l and Thomas Taylor, son ofabseph Taylor, 21, Blacile hurst-street,.all boys, were charged with stealing,a quantity of biscuits, of cheese, and of jam, and nine bottles of sauce, value 108., the property; of Joseph Lawless, Market Hall. They were also charged with stealing, between a', p.m. oni the .3rd inst., and 945 p.m., on the 6th inst., from the stall in the market, of Ann Pickering, ef Crowley, ' Cheshire, a quantity of cheese value Cs., or with ' receiving the same knowing it to have been stolen. The Chief Constable said, Mr. Lawless reported on Saturday morning that robberies from his stall 1101 taken place at different times, within the last ten 1 days,and he missed the articles mentioned from,the Somewhere about 12 o'clock at noon on Saturday,,he was feeling under his stall for something and. got hold I of a lad's leg and was somewhat startled, almost loosing his hold, but dragged the boy out, and found it was one of the Holiwells, the younger of the two brothers. He however wrestled himself assay. Quinn had been in the habit of concealing himself underneath the stalls, and after the gates were closed going to them on an arranged signal from his accomplices, and hand- ing through the articles he had stolen—D. S. Monaghan said Quinn, used to conceal himself under the stalls and remain in the market hall all night, handing out the articles to his comrades, and then run out in the morn- ing after the gates were opened. Two mornings he had watched the men who opened the gates go into the other market, and then ran out with pieces of cheese. The prisoners had hidden some of the cheese in the market and a manhad found it and taken it away.—Quinn said he had " planted " a bottle of sauce in the market but when they went for it it was gene.—Quinn was fined 10s. and sentenced to three days' solitary confinment - in the cells in addition, and the other prisoners were fined ss. each with the same addition to their sentences.

The Cunz reported as to recent prosecutions by the Guardians of parents for cluelty to their children. He added that two o 5 three other cases would be reported by Mr. Shearer, and he advised a prosecution in each case. The moveAuent of the Board in these cases had created terror where something of the kind was needed, and,whilst recommending further proceedings against parents, he also would again suggest the discouragement of begging. He added that pawnbrokers would materi- ally assist to prevent cruelty to children if they either refused to take in pledge articles of bedding and other requisiites or children's clothing, or, when they did take them in pledge, report to some of the Board); officers or the police so that the houses from which the pledges were brought might be promptly visited.—The Rev.G. F. ROBERTS thought this was a very ' good suggestion, and inquired if there was any practical way of carrying it Out.—The CLERK thought it might be included in a general warning note to parents. Owing to times having been rather hard of late, by reason of the weather, they had not been so severe upon the parents, but since the weather was now better they quite intended to prosecute their inquiries and, if they found evidence against people, to prosecute them,whoever they were.—The Rev. G. F. ROBERTS thought the harder the weather the more need there was for the children being looked after properly.—Mr. HEATON said, with regard to the pawning, he had known a case in which a man picked up a cat and went and pawned it. (Laughter.)—Mr. J. Honowrorr : What would he get for a cat P—Mr.HEATow : He got a shilling.—The CLERR said nothing'contributed I more to the state of things which resulted in cruelty to children than the means of pledging children's clothing

..—... . The Clerk reported that the Auditor had since the meeting gone through the accounts of the Union It was now ascertained that the total defalcations of Caldwell, the late Newton relieving officer, were £57 ss, 7d. but agahist this there was a certain aniount which had been due to Caldwell. He would write to the guarantee aociety in which Caldwell was guaranteed.

ABLE-BODIED INMATES.-.THE FARMERS WANT MEIN, In answer to Mr. W. Floughton, the Workhouse Master sad there were 315' inmates in the house.—The Clerk remarked that there had been a material increase all the winter.— olr. W. Houghton said there was a case in the house that ought not to be. That was an abls-bodied man,who ought to be prosecuted for refusing to maintain himself. If he went out he would get work at the first farmhouse he called at.—The man referred to was then called into the Board room. He seemed to be of middle age, and to be enjoying fairly robust health. In answer to queotions, he admitted that he had been in the work- house nine times. On two or three of these occasions, he had been ill or suffering from a broken leg, or some other mishap, and on the other occasions he had, he said "to go somewhere." Mr. Hood-Wright said the farmers could hardly get men, till the Irishmen came back. The man was ultimately told that if he was not out of the house by Friday, he would be taken before the naagis- trates, and he promised to leave the workhouse. DISTRICT NURSES. A letter was read from the Local Government Board empowering the Guardians to appoint district nurses to attend poor patients at their own homes. In the course of a short discussion, some of the Guardians expressed the opinion that such an officer might be useful, but nothing was done in the matter. This was all the business of public interest.
"HE WANTED TO SEE THE WHEELS

GO ROUND." There was once a bright baby boy who loved to ex- amine the internal structure of his uncle's watch in order, as he remarked, that he might "see the wheels go round." Smart and inquiring fellow Some day he may make a watch that will keep better time than those lying Swiss machines—sold in London for thirty shillings—which can with difficulty keep up with the days of 4 the week, to say nothing of hours and minutes. - .

. But for a hundred persons who know how a watch is , constructed, how many know what kind of "works" are inside their own bodies ? Not one. Now the heart is the human pendulum. Sometimes it heats too fast and some- times too slow. What makes it act in that way ? Can you tell ? Probably not. When its irregularity frightens you, you see "a doctov." Why don't you study up the subject yourself; and learn as much about it as any locomotive driver is bound to know about his engine ? Can't? Yes you can. Look here, for instance. A man writes thus: "My heart would throb and beat as if it might -lump out of its I place." The "wheels "' were going much tee rapidly within his body. He wa "gaining time" at a fearful Irate., and when that happens, a man nears his death faster than it ik pleasant to think of. What was wrong with the machinery ? Suppose we look into it and try to fuid out. He says that up to April, 1890, he had always enjoyed
_ gocslhealth. At that date he had an attack of influenza, or the "grip."• This left him in a weak condition, as it commonly does. One morning in the following July, h

found a great patch of eruption, resembling ring-worm, covering his thighs, which gradually spread untd it covered the abdomen and all the lower part of the body. After this his appetite failed, and the natural and neces- sary act of eating caused him great pain ip the chest. He adds : "The wind rolled around my chest and drove all the blood into my head." No. doubt he describes • the sensation correctly, but the fact probably was that there was too little blood in his head rather than to much, and the wind had nothing to do- with it. His system was underfed through the disease, and his bodily machine was, running too fas from very weakness,not from surplus power; just as a ship. rolls and tumbles on the sea from lack of ballast. "t vv3old go into a great heat," he says,." and the pain andl dizziness were so bad that I feared I, should fall down in a ht. At one time my hands and feet were cold and clammy, and at other times they would burn as if stung with nettles. For over three months I continued like this, getting weaXer and weaker every day." Certainly ,what else could be expected? "Feeling now 'very anxious," be proceeds to say,." I saw a doctor, who gave me mediclnes and embrocations, but they were of no use, and I got worse. In August, 1890, it was, I read in the "Freeman's Journal " about Mother Seigel's Syrup,,, and thought it might-possibly help me. I procured a bottle from the Medical Halt, Ballinamore, and to my surprise after taking it I was much better. Further use of the Syrup caused the eruption, or rash, to disappear, and my food began to relish. I could soon eat anything, I was completely cured and was able to work again. I thank God that Seigel's Syrup was made known to. me, and I am, wishful to inform the public outs excellence so other poor sufferers may try it." (Signed) William O'Hara, Lannanarieugh, Bavvnboy,

, Curlough, County Cavan, Ireland. June sth, IE3I, Mr. O'Hara is a farmer, and is well known and res- pected in his district. The ailment he describes was in- digestion and dyspepsia, which produced the palpitation of the heart by the pressure against it of the stomach ; the latter being inflated with gas generated by the fer- mented food. The poison from the same source also entered the blood and threw the brain and nervous system into disorder, thus assisting the general collapse. When Seigel's Syrup had expelled the poison ,and set the digestive machinery once more in motion, strength re- turned as a matter of course, and the heart did its duty regularly and with its natural power. Had Mr. O'Hara understood that all his various aches and pain had one and the same origin he would have been less disconcerted.
The inference seems to be that there is nothing like Mother Seigers Syrup to make the human clock keep time and to repair it when out of order.

A MINUET. About a week after this, Sir Lancelot, returning home after one of his long rides, and proceeding to the sitting-room overlooking the Dutch Garden, which was now Silvia's favourite sanctum, came there upon a very pretty sight. ~ ,

Facing him, a handsome young fellOw in a plum eoloured suit stood by the old spinet,'Which was by the furthest window, and played with great taste and precision one of Haydn's minuets ; while nearer, with her back towards the door, Lady Callerley held out her skirts, and repeated the figures of the stately dance, in an exceedingly graceful manner. But Silvia? Sure this was some fine Court beauty, and not his childish little bride The lady's dress was of silver brocade, with a train of shimmering white satin; pearls were clasped about her round -throat, and twined minongst her russet huir. ' A snowy plume of ostrich feathers nodding above her 'head added height and sdignity to her appearance, and her tiny feet trod rythmically to the slow, stately measure of the music.

div.head: armzemeni
div.p: armzemeni

• Sir Lancelot stopped short in ___ —.went ; but Silvia, catching sight of him in the long mirror opposite, in which she—with a pretty, babyish, innocent vanity, was Watching the reflection of her own charming figure—nodded' gaily„, and called upon him to advance. . 'Came, Lancelot, and dance a minuet with me! aw in in Jack plays divinely, but I am quite lost for ' nt of a partner." r ,She ' held out her hand; as she spoke; but Sir H.Ancelot shook his head. He was too thorough an- Englishman' to be able to 'throw aside f elf-con- famousness, and to enter at a moment's notice into • the spirit of is scene like this. And who on earth r was this young popinjay in, the fine phunreoloured coat and the brocaded vest,, seemingly so very much at home, and upon Such free and easy terms with Silvia? Sir Lancelot, always plain and sober in' his own dress; glanced askance at such a,dandy ; and poor Jack's coat, procured at an 'exceedingly great sacrifice, made a bad, instead a a good im- pression upon him., . . "Nay, Silvia ! I never was a dancing man, and now methinks am getting a trifle stiff in the joints 'for such a pretty pastime! But 'go on 'with your figure, chil.:l, it is very graceful, and pleasant to. look upon!" , !• But Silvia pouted, 'and would Certainly not dance again, since Lancelot did not .think it worth his while to join her ! . When her husband heard who the young fellow in the plum-coloured coat was, he wondered more than ever! On only, pne occasion before had he met young 13reamish, and at that time the latter had been a raw, shy lad of sixteen, blushing and awkward, and shrinking from notice. Sir Lancelot had heard small, good of him since, but had always igetneed him• ass loutish, ill-naannered, and rustic youth; with bloated, sensual teattzes and clumsy gait. Instead, here was a being radiant as a sun god, and graceful, as a young fawn; who appeared quite at ease in a lady's boudoir, and brought wonderful music out of the cracked and jangling strings of the old spinet, never touched since the ,deatii of the last Lady Callerley, Sir Lancelot's !mother. To find such an alteration was a great 'surprise, and, ativinge to say, not altogether a 'pleasauk one. Of course, it was well that Jack should noti be Marie 'and brutal, as thdtongue of popular rumour made' hidi out (if the• baronet had taken the trouble to analyse it, popular rumour in this case might have been reduced to the singular number and the feminine sex) ; but a sharp and sudden' pang had darted through the husband's breast, as he noted how well the young fellow's , grace and sunny expression matched Silvia 's sparkle and gaiety:. Doubtless it' comes rather hard upon a grave, middle-age& Benedict to, have to Confess that another and a younger cavalier is more suited in any way to the girlish bride about whom he himself has, not been without occasional misgivings. Nevertheless, Jack's pleasant manner and frank greeting had its effect, and Sir Lancelot found him- self thawing unconsciously. There were not many people who could resist Jack Brearaish, when he set himself to please. E'en the smart coat faded into insignificance before the simple honest man- hood it covered; for Jack did not live in meek subjection to his clothes; as many people are apt to do, when wearing unusual finery, . . "And why is my little Silvia so gay'?" asked Sir Lancelot, passing his arm around his wife, and leading her ,ut>, to the mirror. She looked herself all over, oriticallY, and then held up her rosy mouth to he kissed, exactly as a child might have done., "Cousin Jack wanted to see my Court dress —we were talking, you know, and he'd never seen 1 any one in, Court dress—and I thought I could show it off beat by putting it on, And after4arcls, when I found he could play, I wished to try how it felt to dance again.. It's ages since I danced, Lance dear, it is indeed! Oh, how I wish Toddy was here —dear Teddy l He is so provoking, but he can dance !" ' . " Teddy would find a country life intolerable ! ' He cannot exist without excitement," returned Sir Lancelot,.drily... He did ..not find it an easy task to induce that pretty sprig of fashion to keep .within reasonable limits, either in the matter of expenditure, or of decorum, and though actual responsibility had ceased, a sense of it still remained behind,, to plague the ex-guardian. These two orphan children of, an old boyish friend,had been a source of 'great care and anxiety to Sir Lancelot Callerley. His co-trustee, a lawyer of lax principles, had got into difficulties a couple of years before • and thereupon proved false to his charge, absconding with the principal part of Silvia:a fortune. 'Teddy escaped the same nusfor- tune through having reached his majority a year previous to , this catastrophe; but was now doing his best to dissipate his portion, not stupendous to
agai

begin with. It was the fashion among young bloods then to fool' away their means upon riotous living, and then to munch their husks with a relish because, forsooth, they had once been talked about. Men of fashion are wiser nowadays. They gi:A in for gambling and matrimony as lucrative professions, and exact the highest interest for their money; because they have grown to recognise that the possession of wealth is power; and that avarice is a very respectable sort of vice, and one that the world condones, if indeed, it does not encourage. "Oh, know he would be moped to death, but I can't help wanting him very much r went on Silvia,, her lips drooping a little at the corners at the thought of her dear scapegrace, "and we could have sneh delightful rides, and he couldn't gamble, and there's no one for him to make love too and altogether he would be so nice and safe. Sir Lancelot smiled, and Jack's brown eyes twinkled.

Are you not envious of so careful a- sister, Breamish ? Not that the youngster would be at, all grateful for such S. paradise I Wait until he gets into some serape, and finds it necessary to rusticate! Then we raay see him here, but cer- tainly not until then, Silvia. In the meantime, my poor little wife will have to put up with her dull husband, and her new cousin ' _ _ _

Callerley bowed courteously to Jack as he spoke, ' but the latter could not help fancying he detected a tinge of irony in the tone: Or was it but a slight emphasis laid upon the word "cousin?" At least, it is certain that something grated on a sensitive ear; and Jack's face flushed -walking home in the twilight, as he recalled it.

One is too apt to imagine that life in the country must, in its unvarying monotony, have been flat, tame, and uninteresting, at a period when there Ivekre no penny posts, no railways, no telegraphs, and ne'daily newspaper's. - After people had exhausted the weather and the crops, besides the gossip and scandal of the neigh- bourhood, one is tempted to ask what on earth they found to talk about? A dozen years later than the time of this story, there was no lack of an interesting and all absorb- ing topic. ,Then it was that the name of Bona- parte was in everyone's mouth. The name—along with the fearsome " bo-boggle " of tire North—was used to terrify and render amenable to discipline, unruly or rebellious

children. "Mind and be good bairns, or we'll send ye ower the sea to Boney '! " was quite a common threat, and one which invariably answered the -purPose- As a matter of constructive imagination, it would be rather curious to know what sort of monster the name conjured up to these threatened, trembling youngsters ! But the_ s_entiment of fear via is_L___lot

any means c onfined to the younger members ot the community. The " bo-bogle " no longer existed for the men and women—save as an unpleasant, blood-curdling, fabled monster, who, having served to make them obedient and subdued, might be safely used as an instrument for good towards their offspring—leit. the all conquering Frenchman was not so ea.sily got -rid of. • • , . • ; It is difficelt to.: realise the tmteeneous, •e which was created when it was rumoured that an - invesien of • our shores by him was imminent. Along the North-east Coast the very places where thelenemy was likely to land were pointed out. Signe and omens of disasters were not warding.' " Falling stars were seen in showers, and predicted, -without doubt, as from time immemorial, the fall • of nations. Visions,of armies were imaged in the sky, waging -mimid warfare. Superstition and ignorance added their quota to the dread which , • , beset country' folk. The great conqueror was victed as possessing every vice Common to humanity, and probably those uncommon also ; in feat, I monste;ip the giAise of than. 1 , ; Those - who 'dared to 'disobey his orders, he ' •- punished by boiling them alive; every morning he bathed in the bleed of his enemies ; nay, more, he was a cannibal, and enjoyed the tender limbs . of sucking infants served up in ragouts or fricassees ;. ; t for breakfast. • - ;Never a night pasaed without a discussion at - Some village gathering as to the probability of an; invasion and a fear lest the dread news of a -;-"ir landing of the enemy should rouse them ere morn- . ing. lie weekly newspaper, brought from the. nearest town with the rest of the marketing, by. the carrier, and read, or rather spelled out, during. . the long winter evenings to an open-mouthed circle of listeners, was full of horrors, and fearsome: accounts of the doings of Napoleon and his army. Not merely to overthrow a dynasty came these , hated foes, but to enslave and to spoil the English pbople. The revolution had shown what brutali- ; ties the French are capable of when roused te frenzy. • • But long before the importance of "Boney " Nees recognised as a disturbing element, there wer'3 stirring events to be chronicled and talked over. The French were the natural foes of all true born Britons, as everybody knew, and was brought to know. • The only subjects of the King who had anY, ;- ~ empathy for foreigners were the free-traders; ana " even their sympathy was strongly tinged with con- , tempt, because in' the matter of contraband goods' • • the suspicious shrewdness and dogged obstinacT Of an Englishman still served to keep an equitable balance of justice; spite of all the jabberings and gesticulations of ,the Johnny Cmpaud who tried and failed—to cheat him. It is difficult to preyeeb oneself despning the persons one_ has succeeded in Aptting the better of, especially when they have Brat tried their best to overreach one. But as for fearing them, the smugglers would not have owned to so great a weakness. There were foes they dreaded, but these were certainly 110 t foreigners. The King's officers were more to be feared than either Froggies or Dutchmen. They were hated like poison by all the fishing and seafaring poPu- lation of our seabound towns and villages. In more than one instance the free-traders were, so unpatriotic as to remain neutral, and lo°' calmly on while their own countrymen got the worst of some naval encounter. On one occasicti a sharp conflict took place between a Freeca privateer and one of His Majesty's ships of war,' within sight of the coast, and this same cordlieu might easily have been decided in favour of tir English, had another vessel cruising, not far '3", condesceuded to come to their assistance.. ,„„ But as the other vessel had been under susPlew- for some time as of smuggling proclivities, it kell a judicious distance, and the prize was lost. An for this seeming pusillanimity there is some ea- °use. ; The ship of war might have left the cargo °n board the smuggling vessel untouched, but sbo would certainly have annexed the crew; at least e° many as were sound and able-bodied. For in those 'perilous times, a man's foes---cer tainly the foes of a sailor or a fisherman—were these 6f his own nation. Quite as much to be; dteaded as any foreign bl" Yemen was the raid Of a press gang. _„a Continuous warfare had thinned our naVI, sailors were greatly in request. (Hear, hear.) The speech of the Prime Minister was a very extraordinary production. It was certainly not lilie the speech one would have expecte& from the first Minister of the Crown delivered upon an occasion such as it was delivered upon, namely, immediately before the meeting of Parliament, to people vreo were looking forward to something of the natere of a- declaration of the policy of the Government. (Laughter and apelausee Ple did not think the country was vnite prepared to adopt that method. It ceuld see perfectly well that when the Tories chase they could move rapidly enongh. It appeared that Lott!' slialiabery had at laeteeame to the conclusion—the Tories died been a long time in coming to it, but they at last admitted that they had arrived at it —that the next ' ,election 'was ganged° be fought upon the sileject Of .flome-Peette. Lord ofielisbury in his following remarks ' was •111,k119 element, because he was never so corn- oaletely in his element as when he was sending a mess- agar:4 hermit to Ireland. (" That's it" and laughter.) lie readetis speech with as much pain and indignation' as he ever:read any speech of a public man in all his life. ' Go -began by endeavearing to stir up since more the I dyingspirie of religious bigotry. Becauseeformotln Eng- i land•was the great Protestant State of the world,therefore Ineand -was not to get Flume Rule. (A. voice: But they will bane it.) Well. he knew Ireland pretty wed, and ,he did not think Lord Salisbury would suc- ceed institheg up religious hate amongst the 7people wise had to live together upon the see of 'lreland. There did net exist, he believed firmly, any religious bigotry or in 4 olerance on the part of the Catholic popu- lation of Ireland at ar—(a pplause)—and indeed he did .not think that outside oil the very small cirdle of 'Ulster it existed either amon,gat the Protestants. The fact that a esubscriptionrstarted for repairs in the e"ro- tester& church and burial -ground in the parish otEene- hal, Where Isaac Butt, whose father was rector of the parisL, lay buried, was mainly contributed to by Catho- lics, was then elted as a psoof of the absence of bigotry among:lrish Catholics. ,Scmee time ago a gentlentao, who had been.apriest in the,city of Cork, was promoted to beiCatholic bishop ef Watulozd. His name was-80. Sheehan. Now, ,Lord Salisbury said that Ireland was the moot ultra-sierical country in the world. Avery -short time ago ,upon Dr. direehan's consecration .as biehon, a numberaof addresses were presented to him. He replied to these., and his reply would give a:514161,0e the class•of men that the Protestants of England were being warned agaiest as being,eirebrands, ready toliey at our throats the moment that ,eme Rule was granted and of the sort of work that was being done by the Catholic priesthood in Ireland, against whom , they were being so constantly warned by Mr. T. W. Russelleend others. eLaughter) The reply 'ef the' bishop was then quoted, which stated that the work of the priest was not bounded by the limits of the sanctuary., tut was far and wide beyond Oman to I take part in such functions of citizenship as he might be called on to diecharge, and to minister to the needs, of the poor that their povertymight be,relieved and. sweet- ened by the ezercises of Christian charity, and to the. needs of the .children above all. the children of watt stud imisfortune. It might be the duty of the priest„ pro- ceeded the bishop, to stand forward in 'come interneseino strife between capital and labour. It was his then te take his place bytbe side of the working-men anil to demand for there that oppression should ceaseef opp me- sion there should be. (Applause.) There was morel in the same strain breathing the same spirit of Chi is- Gan charity. The temark of Mr. J. H. Sugrue, T.P., of Cork, in presenting to the bishop an address from ti4e citizens of Cork was quoted that the address wa joined in by Protestants generally as well as by Cattle-. lies. Dr. Houston asked, if these were the terms upon which Protestants lived with Catholics I in districts where Catholics were in an enor- mous majority, what was the meaning of the impu- tation against the Catholics, and the Catholic priesthood of Ireland that if Horne Rule came it would be used by the Catholic majority to oppress the Protestant minority? (Applause.) There was no truth in the imputation. (" No one doubts that.") It came, he was sorry to say, and he was afraid, from the consciousness of a portion of the Protestants, and especially in Ulster, that perhaps they deserved some degree of retaliation. The Catholics ef Ireland knew very well what the evils of ascendancy were; and they had suffered century after century un- told misfortunes from it, and did not want to and never would try to establish one ascendancy on the ruins of s another. Applause.) They knew perfectly well that a house divided against itself could not stand, and that any attempt to act in the spirit imputed to them would result in the most disastrous failure and the complete disruption of society in Ireland, and bring back a far worse state of things than had existed up to the present time. The idea that anything like protection or any- thing like Catholic ascendancy would be attempted was utterly preposterous, and out of the question. But Lord Salisbury told us that not only were the Irish a most illiterate people, but also that with the exception Of the wealthy people of the districts surrounding. Londonderry and Belfast, they were an uocivilised race. (" Shame and laughter.) If this were true whose fault was it ? (Applause.) If that was the result of seven centuries of conquest and nearly one century of union, that was the strongest argument that could be put for- ward for separation. (Loud applause.) But that was not true. He did not know what civilisation might mean in the dictionary of the house of Cecil. (Laugh- ter and applause.) But if freedom from crime, if purity of life, if unvarying courtesy and hospitality, if public principle andprivate virtue, if learning and piety, constituted civilization, then his (Dr. Houston) 'countrymen were as civilised as any race upon the face of the earth. (Great applause) To say that they were uncivilised was only another way of saying that they were barbarians. (Laughter.) He might tell Lord Salisbury and his 10,000 hearers at Exeter that the Irish people would long remember that, and remember it at the hustings of the next general .election. (Loud applause.) div.head: OPEN INa OF PARLIAMENT.
div.p: OPEN INa OF PARLIAMENT.
tt'OUSE OF LORDS.—_-Tessper.

The seteath session of the twelfth Parliamesst cf the Queen Was opened on Tnesday by commission, the Royal Oommissioners being the Lord Chaacellor, the Duke of Portland, the Earl of Mount-Edgcumbe, the Earl cc! Coventry, and Viscount Cross. The House met at two o'clock. The first peer to arrive was Lord Den- man, and amongst those present when the Lords Com- missioners took their seats in front of the throne were Leeds Cottesloe, Keane, De La Warr Lamington, Bel- more, Dudley, Balfour of Burleigh, Limerick, Stanhope, Camperdown, Percy, Masham, and Waidegrave. Ladies occupied seats in the strangers' gallery,the side galleries, and on the peers' benches. The Speaker of the House of •Commons and the mem- bers of the Lower House were summoned by Admiral Sir James Drummond, and in respense to the summons the Speaker, accompanied by the Sergeant-at-Arms, and numerous members of the House ef Commons, attended the bar of the House. The Royal Commission was then read, after which the Lord Chancellor read the Queen's Speech as follows THE QUEEN'S SPEECH. MY LORDS •ANE GENTLEMYN, I am persuaded that you have deeply participated in the terrible sorrow which has afflicted me and my family in the loss, at the moment when the prospects of his life appeared the happiest, of my dearly beloved grand- son Prince Albert Victor,Duke of Clarence and Avondale. Is has been a solace to us in our grief to have received front all classes and conditions of my subjects, from all parts of my 'Empire as wefi as from all foreign countries the most touching assurances of their deep sympathy under this grievous affliction,and the expression of their affectionateregard and e.ppreeiation for the dear young Prince whom they have lost by this great calamity. My relations with other Powers continue to be friendly. I have lost in the Viceroy of Egypt a loyal ally whose wise government hadin the space of a few years largely contributed to restore prosperity and peace to his coun- try. I have an entire confidence that the same saga- cious policy will be followed by his son, who has been 'named as his successor, in accordance with previous firmans, by Hie Imperial Majesty the Sultan. )in agreement has been concluded with the United States defining the mode in which the disputes as to seal Isheries in Sebring Sea shall be referred to arbitra- tion. 'Zanzibar has been established as a free port by his Highness the Sultan, with my concurrence. I trust that this measure will conduce both to the development of the Sultan's dominions and to the promotion of British commerce on the East African coast. GENTLEMEN OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS, The Estimates for the public service of the ensuing year will be laid before you. They have been prepared with a due regard to financial economy.

MY 140EDS,AND GENTLEMEN, Proposals will be laid before you for applying to Ire- land the general principles affecting Local Government which ha-ve already been adopted in Great Britain, and trust that it may be possible to consider the provisions as to English 'Local Government which, for want of time, it was necessary to omit from the former bill. A measurifor increasing the number of small holdings Of land in agricultural districts in Great Britain will be -submitted for your approval. You will be asked to consider a bill for extending the advantages of assisted education to Ireland, and for other purposes connected with elementary education in that countiy. • A scheme for modifying the existing system of pro- cedure on private bills, so far as it affects Scotland and -Ireland, will be brought before you. A measure will be introduced for the improvement of the Legislative Councils in India. A bill will be laid before you for relieving public ele- mentary schools in England from the present.pressure of Amid rates.

Proposals for improving the discipline of the Estab- lished Church in regard to moral offenees ; for enaoling accused persons to be examined on their trial; for re- vising the existing agreements between the Government -and the Bank of England ; and for amending the law with respect to the liability of erarilorrs for injuries incurred in their employment will also be commended to your attention. ' I pray that Almighty God may guide you in the per- ,formance of your weighty functions. The House adjourned at 2.20. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woo:sack at a quarter past four o'clock. The Duke of Devonshire and Lord Dartmouth took the with and their seat.

The Archbishop of York,introduced by the Archbishop ' co' Canterbury wed the Bishop of London, took tE e oath and his seat on his translation from the diocese of Litch- field. The Bishops of Chester and St. Asaph, Introduced by the Bishops of Oxford and Ripon, also took the oath ad their seats.

div.head: TEIE ADDRESS.
div.p: TEIE ADDRESS.

En the House of Lords the Earl of Dudley mevcd the -Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. He congratulated the Government on its intention te give locs.l government to Ireland, regarded the proposed Small Holdings Bill with great satisfaction, and strongly urged that Irish agricultural labour shculd be more ex- tensively utilised in this country. Lord Lamington, se- conded the Address. The Earl of Kimberley followedonak- ing a. touching reference to the Duke of Olarence's death. Thevroposal to give Local Government to Ireland the received with satisfaction. If it was a good measure it woolo further Home Rule, and if there was little sub- stance in it the Irish people would be dissatisfied sod the Liberal position strengthened. The ~roposal by the Govesninent to increase the number of small holdings was airtriking example that the bidding for the agricul- tural vote was not confined to the Liberai side of the House. Lord Salisbury, in reply, after pathetic allusion to the trince's death, said the hope of the Ciovernment was to make Egypt stand by her own strength, secure enougle.o overcome internal intrigue or rebellion or ex- ternal encroachment. The noble Lord had•oculted with great candour on the coming failure of their legislation for Ireland, but it would be found that their proposals were of.a very soothing character. The Duke of Devon- shire expressed his sympathy with the Royal Family in their bereavement. The Address was agreed to, and their Lordships adjourned at 6.15.

Balfour gave notice that he would on Thursday ask leave to bring in a bill to amend the law relating to Government in Ireland and for other purposes -connected therewith, and also to bring in a bill to amend the procedure in respect to private bills in Ireland and cia Scotland; Mr. Chaplin, that he would on the same day ask leave to introduce a bill to facilitate the acquiai- Con of small agricultural holdings; and Mr. Jackson, that he wouldandso on Thursday ask leave to bring in a bill to improvesaational education in Ireland. Mr. Bal- four also gave notice of his intention to move on Thurs- day that Mr. Be Cobain be required to attend in his plcce on Tuesdar, February 23. , TEX ADDRESS. The Atiressin replyte the Queen's Speech was moved

by Mr. IlEttmoh-Honos. Mr. MILTAIN seconded the motion. Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT said he did not think there was any necessity to make any special remark upon foreign affairs. The House would like to know whether the important bills of the Government were to be read a second time before Easter ; and as to the pro- posed revision of the arrangements between tho Govern- ment and the Bank of England, he asked whether the CiEturcELLos of the EXCHEQUER " meant business or not." As regarded the policy of Local Government for Ireland, the Liberal party would have every disposition to give their support tea genuine and honest measure,but they did not regard the question of Local Government as 4 settling the question of self-government for Ireland. Mr. BALFOUR, after a defence of Lord Salisbury, said he hoped they would make rapid progress with the Small Holdings Bill, and as soon as that measure was in an advanced condition he would propose to read the Irish Local Government Bill a second time and proceed with the other measures. Mr. S. SMITH and Mr. SCHHANN expressed satisfaction at the reference in the Speech to the Indian Councils Bill. Mr. CunzoN said the Bill would be an honest attempt to deal with the question. Mr. James Lowther moved an amendment to the Ad- dress deploring the retention in certain treaties with foreign States of provisions "operating in restraint of the establishment of preferential trading relations amongst several portions of the Empire." Mr. Vincent seconded the amendment. The amendment was nega- tived without a division. The debate was adjourned about half-past seven. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at a quarter past twelve o'clock.

THE ADDRESS. Mr. SEXTON gave notice of an amendment to the Ad- dress acquainting Her Majesty that a decisive majority of the Irish people and of their Parliamentary represen- tatives were convinced of the inability of the Imperial Parliament to legislate for Ireland as that country's dis- tinctive interests required. The debate on the Address was resumed by Mr. BROADHURST, who complained of the manner in which the employers' liability question was dealt with in the Queen's Speech. He said that the Government had shown no indication of earnestness in the matter, and that the mention of the Employers' Liability Bill in the Queen's Speech was a mare farce. Mr. J. W. LOWTHER, replying to Mr. Bryce, said he was glad to say that a complete arrangement had bean arrived at between Her Majesty's Govern- ment and the Government of the United States with re- gard to the Behring Sea question. The points for arbitration had been decided upon, and the Powers who were to be asked to appoint arbitratiors had also been agreed on. These Powers were Italy, France, and Sweden. As to Newfoundland, matters had not advanced very rapidly ; but a draft bill had been prepared, and only awaited introduction to the Newfoundland Legis- lature. With regard to the Slave Trade Conveiation,the Brussels Act had practically been ratified, although the ratification of the Portguese Government had still to be obtained. Mr. Matthews asserted his earnest intentions respecting the amendment of the Employers' Liability Act, and threw blame on Mr. Broadhurst for the Govern- ment's former measure not passing. The debate on the Address was adjourned on the motion of Mr. Chamber- lain.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—Tritrn6DAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at a quarter-past four. FIRST RE&DINGs.--Lord STRATMEDEN and CAMPBELL introduced a bill to abate the smoke nuisance in Lon- don. Lord Cnoss introduced a bill to amend the law relating to certain offices in India. Both bills were read a first time. POLICE PROTECTION AND IRELAND.—The Marquis of LONDONDERRY asked whether it was true that police protection had had to be accorded to Messrs. John Dillon Wm. O'Brien, and T. Healy. Earl CADOGAN said the details asked for by the ez-Viceroy of Ireland were not such as it was cPsirable to discuss within the walls of Parliament. All the police protection that had been afforded to the persons referred to was that which would be afforded to any of her Majesty's subjects. Lord LONDONDERRY said this reply was unsatisfactory. He would at a convenient date raise the question by motion.
The House adjourned at 20 minutes to five. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THURSDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past three. NEW BILLS.-Mr. HOWELL gave notice that he should ask leave to introduce a bill for the better security of the property of corporate associations. Mr. CHANcis gave a similar notice in regard to a bill to amend the law relating to bankruptcies and engage- ments in Ireland.

COUNTY ALDERMEN.-Mr. Walter Long informed Mr. ?Cranes that county aldermen who retire by rotation at the approaching county council elections were eligible for election as councillors at the same elections. _

An inquiry had already been •commenced and WRS being carried on by the medical department of the board with the assistance of pathological and other experts. Ma. div.head: ST. HELENS WATER SUPPLY.
div.p: ST. HELENS WATER SUPPLY.

The scheme for providing the borough of St. Helens with an adequate supply of pure and whole- some water has been advanced another stage during the present week by the commencement of the operations for the erection of buildings and plant at Brownedge Reservoir, Thatto Heath, for the process of improving and softening the quality of the town's water. According to official infor- mation, the hardness of the water varies from seven or eight degrees at the Eccleston Hill and Whislon wells to 22 degrees at Collins Green, while at the new wells at Knowsley and Kirkby the water has 18 degrees of hardness, in addition to a solution of iron. It is only intended to deal with the Knowsley, Kirkby, and Collins Green waters at present, and, after undergoing the softening process, the waters will be run into the Brownedge Reservoir. The Eccles ton Hill and Whiston waters will be pumped direct into the mains for the town, and will join the water from Brownedge Reservoir at a junction of the mains at the Toll Bar and at Factory-row. The proposed new works at Brownedge include the erection of a building 130 feet long by 60 feet wide for the plant, and the total expen- diture will be over £lO,OOO. Mr. John Whittaker, of Sutton, St. Helens, has secured the contract for the building, and Messrs. Woodhouse and Rawson, of Kids- ! grove, Derbyabire. will erect the machinery. The monthly meeting of the Water Committee, was held on Wednesday, Alderman J. M'Bryde presiding. There were also present the Mayor (Coo nCillor Nuttall), Aldermen D. Gamble, J. C. Gamble, Cook, Wilcock, Councillors Johnson (West Sutton), Urmson, Martin, Beecham, Forster, Burchall, Jones, and Walsh. The water engineer (Mr. Gaskin) reported that the total quantity of water distributed had been 76,448,897 gallons ; the daily average being 2,730,316 gallons, against 2,461,540 gallons in the previous month. He also reported that the contractor for the buildings in connection with the new water-softening plant com- menced work on Monday.

OUR Tory. contemporary, the Beaconsfield " Warrington Observer,, " has dis- covered that it was on the wrong scent in,seeking to make out that Dr. HOUSTON, the Liberal candidate for Warrington, was at one , time a TOry. But there ism° expression of regret for having been party to &gross misrepresentation of the character of an honourable and consistent man. That is not the Tory way. The Tories claim to constitute the party of gentlemen ; but it always happens in such matters that they felt° justify the claim. Incidentally, the late Lord BNA- CONSFIRLD was referred to by Dr. liousrox,.who was wrongly said to have spoken of him as a friend, being,, like many other politicians, ofkopinion that he was apolitical adventurer, who was without principle. The virtuous " Observer " is quite shocked at this expression, of opinion; and advises people to read the life of Lord BEACONSFIELD.. For ourselves we have done more than read it : we have studied it ; and, since the issue is raised, we do not hesitate to say there never,was a politician of emin- ence more deserving to be styled an adventurer with, an utter disregard of principle. It is desir- able,.,of course, to have authority for such a state- ment, and it is all the better when the authority cannot be gainsaid by those who raise objection. Whien Lord BEACONSFIELD (then MT. Disraeli) sought to " dish the Whigs" by bringing in a fancy frenchise bill, Lord SALISBURY, as a high and dry Tory, was so disgusted with this sudden change of Rront that he described statesmen who were guilty of such pranks as "politicaladventurersrand their , manoeuvres as "a, policy of legerdemain." Dr. HOUSTON is, therefore, at one with the present Prime Minister in his estimate of the character of the idol of the Primrose League; and the "Observer "is in the unhappy position of co 'demning Lord SALISBIIRM when it condemns the Liberal candidate for Warrington. The fact is it is the Tories who know /east about the "Life of Lord BEAcomm.nan "who are loudest in his praise; and they have a pepfect representative in that fervent butbelated admirer, who, after responding to the callof " Three cheers for Beaconsfield," ex- claimed ".Three cheers for Disraeli." Poor man ! Efe didn't know his favourite under his new title.

But, to carry tle matt& a step further, those who have read the life of Lord Beaconsfield can- not have forgotten that be did a great many things which are completely at variance with regard for principle. He commenced his career as a Re- former, and joined the Westminster Reform Club; but when he had turned his coat he had the audacity to affirm that it was a club he had "never heard of." On another occasion he pro- nounced a striking eulogy on Wellington, a great part of which was stolen from the French of M. Thiers„ The late Mr. Bright once charged kira with having written something which counten- anced regicide ; he indignantly denied the charge; but was convicted of paltering with the truth when the following lines were quoted from his "Revolutionary Epick :"

_ _ Pharoah's doom Shall cool those chariot wheels now hot with blood; And blessed be the hand that dares to raise The regicidal steel that shall redeem A nation's sorrow with a tyrant's blood. He attacked Sir ROBERT PEEL in the most bitter fashion, because that great statesman adopted Free Trade principles; and then turned round
