div.p: THE UNITED ALKALI COMPANY AND THEIR WEIGHTS.

The adjourned summons against the United Alkali Company, Limited, for being in possession of ten 581 b weights which were light and unjust should have been hard at Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, but as Alderman Maspratt, who was on the bench is interested in the Company, the case had to be again adjourned. PETROLEUM OIL.—J. S. Garland, Ironmonger, Bridge-et., Warring on.—Advt.

CONCERT AT PAGE LANE MISSION Room, WIDNES, On Thursday evening an excellent concert was given by the St. Ambrose Glee society, of which Mr. W. White is the conductor, on behalf of defraying the cost of a piano for the St. Ambrose Mission room, The Rev. G. A. Le Bert presided. The programme was opened by the St. Ambrose String Band playing "The Triumphal March." The other drtistes were as follows :—Misses S. Wade, F. M. White, M. Foster Messrs. J. Perks, J. R. Lea, J. Norris, E. M. Harrison, J. Poole, W. Whar- ton, and E. and L. Foster (humourists). UMBRELLAS BECOVERrD.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-et., Warrinoon.—Advt. PIG KEEPING AT RUNCORN,

Before Mr. Charles Reynolds and Mr. James Handley, at Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, W. Probin, of Wickston Hill, Runcorn, was summoned for keeping pigs in such a position and condition as to be injurious to health. Mr. Lake appeared on behalf of the .Board of Commissioners, and Mr. Percival, nuisance inspector, proved the case. It was alleged that filth Rowed from the pigcote on to the road in front of some cottages and caused a dangerous nuisance. Mrs. Probin said the pigs were kept as clean as possible. They had given away some and sold others, and the last one would be rem- oved at noon that day. The Bench made an order prohibiting the defendant from keeping pigs in that place in the future. CHARGE AGAINST A RUNCORN CHEMIST.

Mr. Peter Smith, chemist and druggist was sum- nioned to the Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, to answer a charge of assaulting and beating his:wife, Mary Anne Smith, on the 28th January. Mr. Murphy, solicitor,. Liverpool, said he appeared for the com- plainant. He had received a telegram, and he believed also that one had been sent to the Superintendent saying that Mr. Smith was seriously ill. Apart from that he had arranged, subject to their worships' position with Mr. Neild,the defendant's solicitor, for an adjourn- ment of the case for a week. If their worships could allow the case to stand over fo- a week it would be con- venient for all parties.—The Superintendent had no objection and the Bench adjourned the case. KITCHEN RANGER.9.—Garland Builders Ironmonger, War- rington.— Advt. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD. The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday after- noon, at the Cemetery. Mr. H. Coleburn presided, and there were present Messrs. Imison, W. Littler, F. Hand- ley, Mellor, Whittaker, and Salkeld (sec.) It was re- ported that during the ten months ending January 25th there were 427 intertnents, an increase of 20 on the cor- responding period last year. The fees received amounted to £3BB 13s. Bd., a decrease of £4 12s. Bd. Accounts amounting to £lO 15s. 6d. were passed for paymeiat,and a cheque was drawn in favour of the Runcorn Board of Commissioners for £350 on account of the expenditure incurred by them in draining and making Victoria-road, subject to the sanction of the Lords of the Treasury. The Secretary was instructed to make arrangements for the loan of £533 6s. Bd. for a term of 20 years, to be re- paid by annual instalments. RE-VALUATION of STOCK. Unheard :of Bargains, at Evan' 17, Sankey-street, Warrington,—.Advt.

HOLY TRINITY CHURCH RUNCORN. The annual tea party was held in the Schoolroom on Thursday evening. About 150 persons were present. At the concert afterwards there was a crowded audi- ence. The Rev. Dr. Preston, who presided, said in the course of his speech that the attendance at Church was not what it ought to be and he urged them to make an effort to attend more regularly. The chief event of the year had been the bazaar which realised £275 and the majority of the committee apportioned £3O of this to the Church, and £2O to Pastoral Aid Society and Church Missionary Society and the balance went to the schools. The Church was in need of a considerable outlay to put it in good repairs ; the roof at present was only kept from certain collapse by a pillar erected by Mr. C. Timmins In the Provident Club there was a balance of £99.-1n the course of the evening, a varied enterainment of songs, glees, Frc., was giyen by local vocalists. UMBRELLAS RECOYERED,—J. and W. The re- port stated that the consumption of gas continued to in- crease satisfactorily,and it had not been found necessary, in spite of the high price of coal, to charge a higher rate for gas. The revenue account showed a balance of £4,208 6s. 4d., out of which the directors recommended a dividend of £lO per cent.per annum,leaving the sum of £2OB 6s. 4d. to be added to the profit and loss account, the balance of which, after payment of dividend, would be £697 15s. 4d. and the Reserve fund £3,354 2s. CONSERNATIVB BALL AT RUNCORN. - _ _

The annual Conservative ball tc)lc place in Runcorn Public Hall, on Tuesday evening, and was attended by much success. The hall had been charmingly decorated for the occasion by Mrs. Lightburn, Mrs. Martin, Mrs. Abel, and Mr. A. Lightburn, and a few friends. The orchestra was set off by a number of flowering and foliage plants from the conservatories of Mr. P. Speak- man, C.C., and Mr. J. W. Lightburn. About 70 couples were present, and dancing, which commenced at eight o'clock, was kept up until two o'clock. The music was supplied by Mr. J. W. Temperley's band, and the manner in which their part of the programme was performed called forth universal praise. Mr. J. J. W. Potter ably fulfilled the duties of M.C., and the stewards were Messrs. G. Sumrnersfield, J. J. Speakman, G. Burrows, Geo. Hewitt, A. Lightburn, and Peter Hopwood. The refreshment department was in the hands of Mrs. Gerst, of High-st., and during the interval many of the guests sat down to an excellent supper. BvsN's GREAT STOCKTAKING SALE now on.-17 Sankey- st., Warrington. BRUTAL KICKING CASE AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, Jas.. McCamley of 3, Marsh-st., Widnes, was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial, on a charge of unlawful wounding Jane Oliver, a woman with whom he cohabited. From the evidence it seemed that when the prisoner arrived home on Saturday at noon the woman was under the influence of drink and he abused her in a most dreadful fashion. He knocked her to the ground and then kicked her with his clogs in almost every part of the body and left her. Afterwards he left the house and Oliver went to bed. At three o'clock he returned, and dragged the woman out of bed and repeated his brutal conduct. The woman's screams attracted the attention of the neigh- bours.—Dr. Hutchinson informed the magistrate (Mr. Burchall) that both the woman's eyes were black and completely closed, and blood had been oozing out of them Her face was swollen and she complained of pains in the back. Her legs were t erribly bruised pieces of flesh were attached to her stockings, and in one place the stocking was embedded in the flesh. All parts of her body bore evidences of the violent treatment she had received. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-St.. Warrington.— Advt.

div.head: DEAD IN A DITCH NEAR WIDNES.
div.p: DEAD IN A DITCH NEAR WIDNES.

Mr. Brighouse, the county coroner, yesterday week held an inquest at Farnworth, on the body of Sara Kelly, single woman, 62 years of age, who had lived in Caroline-street, Widnes. On the Wednesday she was found dead in a ditch in Norlands-lane. Dr. Tyrer of Rainhill, who had made a post mortent, said the cause of death was apoplexy.

div.head: WIFE DESERTION AT RUNCORN.
div.p: WIFE DESERTION AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn police court on Wednesday, by Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. G. L. Davies, Thomas Hulse, flatman, Weston Point, was char.led with having deserted his wife and two children, on the 9th October, 1891.--Mr. W. Howard, deputy relieving officer said the defendant's family had cost the Guardians £2B.—The prisoner was sentenced to a month's hard labour.

A TRAMP AND HIS QUARTERS. William Rowlands, a stranger, was brought before the Runcorn magistrates, on Wednesday, charged with sleeping on the Ship Canal Rope Works, Bottom Locks, and with having no visible means of support. It was proved that the prisoner had been striking matches in the place, which was a very dangerous proceeding. He was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour.
UNIVERSITY EXTENSION _LECTURE AT _RUNCORN.

The third of the series of lectures on the History of Florence was delivered on Monday evening, in Bethesda schoolroom by the Rev. W. Hudson Shaw. There was a good attendance. The lecturer dealt with Florence in the 14th century in a highly interesting and instructive manner, and the many beautiful views exhibited by the limelight lantern enhanced the value of the lecture.

THE SUBSIDENCE QUESTION. The Local Government Board inquiry into the proposals to form either one large compensation dis trict or several small ones in Cheshire to cover the area in which subsidences have occurred through the pumping of brine was resumed at Northwich on Thursday. A large number of landowners in the neighbourhood of that town are in favour of the whole of the salt field being made into one district, but their proposal is opposed by the Winsford Local Board and other similar authorities, on the ground that the pumping at Northwich is alone responsible for the damage at Northwich,and that consequently only the brine pumpers there ought to be asked to pay for it. The inquiry was again adjourned. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. LIVERPOOL ENGINEERING SOCIETY. The eighth ordinary meeting of the present ses- sion was held on Wednesday evening. at.the Royal Institution. Mr. Thomas Morris, F.G.S., read a paper entitled "Engineers' tests for iron con- sidered, and suggestions for standard uniform tests." The author showed by tables of numerous 1 engineers' tests how engineers would ask for diff- erent tensile strains for same class of work, adding that the iron must be equal to some known "brand." as though the iron produced in the local- ities named were uniform in quality. He paid a high tribute to the reduction of area test, as being one that gave more consolation to the engineer in case of work coming to grief than any other test specified. The elongation test, which, he said, was I only another form of test for ductility, was not to be depended upon with the same ease and comfort as contraction of area; and the manner in which the former tests was specified by nearly all eng- ineers, was anything but creditable. He treated the "limit of elasticity " test with behaviour al- most amounting to ridicule. His suggestions for "standard uniform tests and conditions were put in the simplest form, and were thoroughly ex- plained to those present. The paper was very well I received by the large number of members present, and the discussion was adjourned to the next meeting.

div.head: MR. WADE, DEACON FOR
div.p: MR. WADE, DEACON FOR
WIDNES DIVISION.
LIBERAL MEETING AT WIDNES.

Under the auspices of Widnes Division Liberal Association,a public meeting was held in the Baths Assembly-room, Widnes, on Monday evening, under the presidency of Mr. Eustace Carey. The room was crowded, and on the platform were Mr. H. Wade Deacon, the candidate, Major Wareing, Alder- man E.K. Muspratt, C.C., Messrs. T. Snape, C.C., S. Deacon, F. Hartland, Rev. R. G. Hughes, and Mr. 11. B. Shores, secretary and agent. Letters of apology for non-attendance were read from Mr. T. Sutton Timmis and Mr. W. B. Bowring, Liberal candidate for Abercromby Division. . . _

The Chairman said at every meeting which was held in furtherance of the candidature of Mr. Deacon more enthusiasm was evinced, and they were more hopeful of his success as time progressed. As Liberals they had also cause for encouragement in the awkward difficul- ties their opponents sometimes got into when they ven- tured upon making speeches on the political situation. He expected Widnes to follow the grand example of South Moulton, and Rossendale, and return Mr. Deacon by a triumphant majerity. (Cheers.) Alderman Muspratt proposed a resolution of confidence in Mr. Gladstone and expressing the hope that he would be spared to grant Home Rule to Ireland. After dealing with the recent utterances of Lord Salisbury, the speaker said the secret of the Tory opposition to Home Rule was that they feared that orea) Home Rule was granted to Ireland. democratic legislation for England would follow. (Cheers.) As to Mr. Chamber- lain's pension scheme for poor men over 65 years that was useless and was meant to divert the attention of the people from the real issue of the approach- ing election. (Hear, hear,) He (Mr. Muspratt) would be glad to see every man getting a pension but where was the money coming from ? Not from the pockets of Mr. Chamberlain or Lord Salisbury, but by taxing the people. They could not get a gift frem Gov- ernment unless it was taken from the taxpayer and the taxpayers of England were the working men. Mr. Chamberlain did not always speak thus of' the taxes. Before he joined the Tory ranks he suggested that the country was too heavily taxed and that the taxes should be put upon the richer men. (Applause.) Mr. Mus- pratt described the Allotment Act as a complete failure and said to be successful it must be worked by Parish Councils and not left in the hands of large landowners, but to the labourers of the villages. (Cheers.) Mr. Snape seconded the resolution and said the en- thusiasm shown at Widnes reminded him of Rossendale. They had a splendid candidate, an excellent cause and a first class agent (cheers) and he expected Mr. Deacon to be returned at the head of the poll at the coming elec- tion. (Cheers.) Mr. Deacon, who had a most enthusiastic reception, supported the resolution. After making a reference to the hearty reception he had met with in all parts of the division, he said they had a hard fight and they must leave no stone unturned under which lay a vote if they wanted to win next time. They must endeavour to convince those men who were on the balance, and had not made up their mind which way to vote, and if each individual Liberal would do his best to induce some friend or acquaintance to vote for their cause they would win. (Hear, hear.) One reason for thinking they would win was that sine ) 1886 there had been vacancies in 122 different constitu- encies. In 1886 the conservatives and Unionists held 74 seats between them, whilst the Liberals and the Irish Nationalists held 48. In 1892 the Tories held 54 seats and the Liberals 68. In lery Lancashire there had been eleven by-elections since 1886. In that year nine of the seats in question were held by the ministerial party, and two by the Liberals. Now five were held by the minis- terialists, and six by the Liberals, (Cheers.) That showed that the tide was running in their favour. They must also tell doubtful voters that at the first election Mr. Moss won by 1,677, and at the second, on the same register, by 794 votes. Since then the number of voters I had considerably increased, especially in Widnes, and just as the Tories looked upon Garston as their strong- hold, so they looked upon Widnes. Therefore, the larger the increase in Widnes, the better for the Liberal party. There was a great feeling of hopefulness in the division amongst Liberals, and they were anxious for another opportunity of testing the feeling of the voters at the poll. (Cheers.) Dealing with the Home Rule question, the speaker said the next Government would be Liberal,and Home Rule was certain. They had at this election to fight the same old battle against injustice and inequality. He did not expect all men to be equal ir, the immediate future, for God had constituted men differently—some were intellectual giants, others were physical giants,and no two men were alike; but while he agreed with such an inequality as that, and knew that it would never be done away with,yet the inequalities which were broalght about by the legislation of men could be swept away for ever. The Liberals had removed many obstacles, but it was the Tories' plan to abuse the Liberal programmes and then adopt them. (Applause.) The Tories wanted to extract the vital essence from the Liberal programme, but it would do them no good. One man one vote was one of the steps which the Liberals were taking to bring about a more equal state of affairs. Mr. Moss said that the Tory Land Bill would bring peace to Ireland, but it had not done so. The population had decreased, and many of them had come over to England. Why? Because of the unjust laws of the landlord, and because the English legislation had practically destroyed the Irish industries. If Ireland could support eight millions of people 50 years ago. why couldn't she to-day? He (Mr. Deacon) believed she could if the people governed themselves. It was their duty, as well as to their interests, to make it possible for the Irish people to live at home, instead of coming over to England. The same problem faced them in England, the people were leav- ing the agricultural districts and going into the towns. No one could blame the people for doing this, but it would be better for the whole country if they could be persuad- ed to stay on the land. This would have to be done by forming Parish Councils. He believed in trade organisa- tions, although they sometimes made mistakes, yet they had done a great deal for the workingmen. There was some things, such as the control of the post office, pen- sions, eight hours labour day and others, which would not be carried on by municipalities, but must be attended to by the Government. He mentioned these in order to make his thoughts plain to everybcdy. He did not wish to gain one single vote by concealing his opinions. (Cheers.) Mr. Lawrence Gene, Q.C., M.P., also supported the resolution and in the course of his speech said he held it was man's duty to improve his position as much as pos- sible in this life, and to make this world as much a heaven as possible. When Chr:st was on earth lie taught the people that they must look after their bodies as well as their souls. He believed Mr. Gladstone would live to carry out his great work of improving the condi- tion of the working classes ; but if he were not spared, there were other men who had received virtue from him who would carry on the work which he had begun. (Cheers.) In conclusion he strongly advocated Mr. Deacon's candidature.---The resolution was carried unan- imously. On the proposition of Major Wareing a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Gene and a similar compliment was paid to the Chairman on the motion Of Mr. Gene seconded by Mr. F. Hartland.

div.head: RUNOORN,S REPRESENTATIVES ON THE COUNTY COUNCIL '
div.p: RUNOORN,S REPRESENTATIVES ON THE COUNTY COUNCIL '
LIBERAL MEETING AT RUNCORN.

, • On Wednesday evening a meeting of Liberals convened by •Mr. John Clark and Mr. Alfred Riley, the Runcorn District County Secretaries,was held in Union Hall, Regent-street, for the purpose of consid- ing the attitude of the Liberal party in reference to the approaching Cheshire County Council Election. and to take such measures' as might be decided upon. There was a good attendance and Mr. J. R. Frith was voted to the chair. After some prelimin- ary observations, Mr. B. Bniveton said the parties in the County Council were so evenly balanced that neither party could take advantage of the other. As they were aware, the Aldermen who were coming out this year were all Liberals and if the Liberal party did not take care they might find the Conser- vative party with a majority at the next election, which was a state of things they did not look for- ward to with any amount of pleasure. He believed the Liberal patty would take no undue advantage of their positions if they were in a majority; he was not so certain that they could say that much for the Tories. There were some honourable men but there were others of whom they could not say much good. What should they do to strengthen the Lib- eral party in the County Council. The present repre- sentation of Runcorn was not satisfactory. HR. CHARLES lIAZLEHURST went in as an independent candidate and his votes had all gone Conservative,and they would do. Were they as Liberals going to assist a Conservative to the County Council ? It would be the greatest folly, and the Liberal members of the Council were looking to Runcorn to strengthen their position at the next election and he felt sure if the Liberal party put its shoulder to the wheel it could return a good Liberal for Runcorn North. (Ap- plause.) Now came Runcorn South. WERE THEY SATISFIED WITH. MR. SPEAKMAN P

Candidly he must confoss 114-3--;v;;.nOt satisfied with him. What he was about to say he should have said had Mr. Speakman been present and he was speaking of him only in his public capacity. In the first place his Liberalism was not sound. He knew the opinion of the County Councillors was that he was always sitting on the hedge ; that they never knew were he was going ; and he believed if the opinions of the Liberal members of the Council were polled they would prefer a Tory being re- turned for Runcorn South rather than Mr. Speakman. There was a meeting of the Cheshire Liberal Federation at Crewe, the other day to which the Liberal County Councillors were invited but Mr. Speakman was not pre- sent. The question of re-election of aldermen was dig-

to contest the seat in the interests of the Liberal party. —Mr. CartwriT.ht seconded.—Mr. Handley said they must be careful that the contest was on proper party lines, and not on personal grounds between man and man. He had drawn up a few questions on matters that were likely to come before the Council in future aid that views of all the candidates might be asked upon them.—Mr. Watson said they could not have any stronger candidate than

MR. SAMUEL TAYLOR and he had great pleasure in moving that he be asked to contest the seat.—Mr. Clegg said he did not think Mr. Taylor would stand,but if he would he should have great pleasure in seconding the resolution.—Mr. Jas. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Timperley said he had every reason to be- lieve that Mr. Taylor would stand if he were asked. (Hear, hear.) He would be a very straightforward candidate.— Mr. Billington thought

MR. SPEAKMAN A GOOD LIBERAL and he should be loth to go against hirn.—Mr. Ben Cros- by was of the same opinion. He thought they ought to get to know the views of Mr. Speakman, and then they would know what to decide.—Mr. Holt said Mr. Speak. man was not returned by the Liberals.—Mr. Lea said at the meeting on the previous Friday Mr. Speakman said he was willing to work with the Liberals and he thought that was sufficent.—Mr. Kniveton said for years Mr. Speakman had taken no part in politics—Mr. W. The speaker described Mr. Speakman as neither Liberal I nor Tory.—Mr.Millington said Mr.Speakman had utterly discredited his Liberalism by his action in the County Council.—Mr. Handley said Mr. Speakman had been a member of the Liberal Association for years, and it was possible that if he were asked upon policy he would be able to satisfy them that he was a good Liberal. Having done that they would be able to count upon his votes in future. As to Mr. Taylor he had said when Mr. Ockles- ton's name was mentioned that he would not stand for the North but if there was a vacancy in the South he did not mind contesting a small division like that.—fhe motion was then put to the vote and

MR. OCELESTON WAS ADOPTED by a substantial majority.—Mr. Kniveton proposed that they have a contest in the south, and that Mr. S. Taylor be asked to become the Liberal candidate.—Mr. Betney seconded. div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting was held at D'utton Workhouse on Tuesday. Mr. Mclntyre presided, and there were present Rev. J, W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Aaron, Stokes, Edwards, Parr, J. Baguley, Weir, Heywood, Brandreth, Bretherton, J. Ashton (clerk), G. Ashton (deputy clerk), J. Farrington (nuisance inspector).
THS POLLUTION OF THE MERSEY AND IRWELL.- IMPORTANT BILL.

Mr. J. Lyon Whittle, town clerk tif Warrington, called the attention of the Authority to the River Mersey and Irwall (Prevention of Pollution.) Bill which the joint Committee intend to promote in the next session of Par- liament. The object of the Bill, as recited in the Bill, was to remove the restrictions contained in the Rivers ' Pollution (Prevention) Act 1876. Perhaps the most im- portant of these restrictions as affecting districts situate on the tidal part of a river was that contained in the definition of" stream" in section 20 of the Act of 1876, and which would be lost if the Bill became law in its present form. Clause 3of the Bill rendered every Sani- tary Authority within the jurisdiction of the Joint Com- mittee liable to heavy penalties if they allowed any liquid sewage matter or any poisonous matter or pollut- ing liquid proceeding from any manufactory or manu- facturing process to be carried into any river or stream. He had asked the Clerk of the Joint Committee to agree to the following sub-section being added to that section "This section shall not apply to any tidal waters which have not been determined by the Local Govern- ment Board to be a stream under Section 20 of the Rivers Pollution (Prevention) Act 1876." The Corpora- tion had no objection to any other provisions of the Bill, on the contrary, they were desirous of supporting it as the Borough had longsuffered from the polluted condition of the river which in its course through the heart of the town, carries with it all the filth and sewage of the many towns above the borough. It did occur to him that the Joint Committee should begin where the pollution of the river commenced and deal with each district in its turn down the river, and when the districts on the tidal part were reached in their proper order will be the time to apply to the Local Government. Beard to deal with the river under section 20 of the original Act. He hoped the Sanitary Au hority would support the action taken by the Corporation and which if agreed to by the Joint Committee, would avoid any Parliamentary opposition with its consequent expense.—The Clerk said Mr. Whittle had not sent a copy of the Bill, but it appeared to him from reading that letter that they would be prevented from turning sewage into the tidal portion of the Mersey, if the Bill passed. He suggested that a copy of the Bill should be obtained and then they could fully consider the subject and the attitude they would take.—Mr. Aaron moved that the Clerk obtain a copy of the Bill and the motion was carried.

div.head: INFLUENZA.
div.p: THE INFLUENZA.

The Clerk read a circular letter issued by the Local Government Board with regard to influenza and the pre- cautions to be taken to prevent infection.—Mr. Stokes said the suggestion might be improved by the addition of one asking people who were recovering from the disease not to recklessly expose themselves. fie related an incident where a whole family had been struck down with the disease through a man returning to work before he had completely recovered. One member of the family had died and another was a complete wreck. The medi- cal men ought to be requestad to caution their patients not to mix with other people until they had completely recovered.

A CANAT., NUISANCE AT WESTON POINT. A letter was read from Mr. W H. Collier, manager of the Manchester Ship Canal Company, complaining; of a nuisance arising thrcugh sewage being turned into the Runcorn and Weston Canal from a number of cottages in Sandy-lane. He wished the Guardians to prevent the turning of the sewage into this canal.—The Inspector said there was a syphon under the canal at this point, and he believed it belonged to this Authority, but it was at present out of order.—Mr. Aaron said when the hot weather came this nuisance might be a very serious one. He held that the syphon belonged to the Ship Canal Co. Re suggestsd that a committee consisting of Messrs. Stokes, Baguley, add himself should meet on the spot, and deal with the question, and that the Clerk, Inspec- tor, and Medical Officer should be in attendance.—Mr. Weir seetinded.—Carried.
TEE WATER SUPPLY OF SUTTON.

The Inspector reported that in accordance with in- structions he had obtained an estimate for sinking the public well to a still further depth. Mr. C. De Prez ten- dered to sink the bore hole a further depth of nine yards and other work at a cost of £53. The cost up to the present time was £65, and if the other work were carried out the total cost would be £ll5. The water was over 14,5 f t. from the surface.—Mr. Aaron said the owners of the property and not the ratepayers ought to find that water, and as the ratepayers had not been consulted in the matter he contended that the overseers could not legally levy a rate upon them,and if he were a ratepayer in the township he would not pay.—The Board could not spend over £5 without a contract.—The Clerk said he knew nothing to prevent the Board.—The Inspector said the pump was a public one and it was the duty of the Authority to do their best to supply it with water, but the Authority having spent a reason- able amount could now abandon the project and call upon Mr. Talbot, the landlord to supply the people with water.—Mr. Aaron proposed that the ' well be abandoned and the owners called upon to provide water.—Mr. Heywood said this was the same as all water schemes. In the first instance it was only to cost £lO or £l5 and now there was no guarantee that £ll5 would complete it.-112 reply to questions, Mr. Farrington said this well was not within a reasonable distance of many occupiers. About 11 occupiers were dependent on this well. The supply of water to the village was not satis- factory and he believed that the large amount of sickness there was attributable to drinking impure water from the road side wells which merely contained surface drainage.—Mr. Parr seconded Mr. Aaron's motion.—Mr. , Heywood moved an amendment that the township

Committee be strengthened by the addition of several members of the Authority and that a ratepayers' meeting be called to consult with the owner of the property- or his agent. —Mr. Weir seconded. The original motion was carried by five votes to four.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutta Workhouse on Tuesday. Mr. Mclntyre presided,and there were present the Rev.J. W. N. Tanner. Messrs. Weir, J. Baguley, Aaron, Stokes, Lea, Edwards, Bretherton, J. W. Baguley, Farrington,Baxter,Gey- wood, Parr, J. Ashton (clerk), G. Ashton (deputy clerk.)

div.head: COUNTY ACCOUNTS.
div.p: THE COUNTY ACCOUNTS.

A letter was read from Mr. Reginald Potts,clerk to the County Council, stating that the Finance Committee had considered the application of the Board for the supply of a copy of the County Accounts to each Guardian of the Union, and regretted that they could not see their way to colhply with the requests.—Mr. Parr : I always thought that would be the answer.—Mr. Stokes : They would have to serve other Unions the same and it would be a great expense.—Mr. Parr : They might spend the money worse.— Mr. Brandreth : Then let us know how the money is spent.

div.head: WOMEN AS GUARDIANS.
div.p: WOMEN AS GUARDIANS.

The Clerk had on the table the tenth annual report of the Association for returning women as Poor Law Guar- dians.—Mr. Parr : We want that read, sir. (Laughter.) —Mr. Lea : You will have to start meetings at eight o'clock in the morning then. (Laughter.)—Mr. Stokes : Pass it on to the Runcorn Guardians ; they have a seat or two to spare. (Laughter.)

TEE COUNTY EXPENDITURE.—IMPORTANT STATEMENT. Mr. Brandreth proposed the passing of accounts, amounting to £319 103. 11d., as recommended by the Finance Committee. He said there was a balance in the treasurer's hands of £3,384 15s. 2d., and they had a precept from the County Council of £3,291 ss. id., which was due on the 30th January, and which ought to have been paid. This call was for the half-year and was made up as follows :—County rate, £2,308 16s. 7d. ; constabulary, general expenditure, £230 163. 10d. ; con- stabulary, local expenditure, £751 us. Bd. The board had not sufficient money to pay this amount, after pay- ing the accounts passed that day, and the County Council would have to wait until the next calls were due. The county rate was increasing at a rapid rate, and it was time that some expression of opinion should go to the public. (Hear, hear.) They were about to be called upon to elect a fresh body of county councillors.—Mr. Parr : I would not have one of the old ones in. (Laugh- ter.)—Mr. Aaron : How do you know you will get the calls in to pay this bill ? Weston will not pay theirs.— Mr. Brandreth said it was all very nice for the County Council to send these precepts, and then they had to call upon the overseers for the money. Not one-tenth of the money collected under the name of the poor rate went to the poor, which was very misleading to those who had to pay. The union did not spend the money, it was spent by the County Council, and the people ought to I know that. He found from a report issued that from 1876 to 1886, when the quarter sessions had con- trol of the county, the average annual expendi- ture was £96,000, and for three years immediately before the County Council took control the average ex- perditure was £llO,OOO. Since the County Council had tal en the matter in hand the average income and ex p. -iture had been £250,000. (Sensation.) The Chair- man of the County Finance Committee asserted that this was evidence of the onerous and numerous duties the Council and its officers had to perform. Mr. Bran- dreth said that the expenditure on the highways was one great cause of this excessive figure. A total of L 40,000 was spent on the roads,and Mr. Joseph Beckett, a silk mercer, of Chester, was the chairman of the Highways Committee—(" What does he know about stone ?")—and he had been made a magistrate since he was appointed to the head of that Committee. Now, Lord Egerton had stated that political affairs had no- thing to do with the Council, but he (Mr. Brandreth) noticed that the gentleman who had issued addresses referred to political feelings, but said not a word about expenditure, and he wished that some of Mr. Beckett's political friends would call his attention to it.—He alleged that much money was wasted on the Council.— Mr. Aaron: Mr. Beckett has got made a magistrate for making good roads.—Mr. Brandreth pointed out that ia the adjoining county of Denbigh the County Council had managed the affairs at less cost than the magistrates.— The Chairman : I wish Mr. Brandreth had a seat on the County Council.—Mr. Parr: I think it would be a good thing to petition Parliament to do away with County Councils altogether.—Mr. Heywood : Send new men next time.—Mr. Parr : I would send everyone new men next time.—The Chairman ruled thc discussion out of order, and it ceased.

div.head: AN INSURANCE DISPUTE.
div.p: AN INSURANCE DISPUTE.

Mr. Aaron drew attention to the case of a woman named Haley who had become chargeable to the Union, whose husband died last year. He was insured in the Victoria Legal Friendly Society, but because the widow who was the man's third wife gave his age a year differ- ent from that given by himself the Society paid him £7 short cf the coin assured. No birth or baptism certifi- cate of the man could be found, and the Society were no more able to prove that the man had given a wrong age than it could be proved right, and as they had ac- cepted the premiums without question for over 30 years, they ought to have paid the money due. As the widow was now receiving relief, he moved that the Guardians bring an action to recover the money.—The Clerk said the Society took the certificate of death as conclusive proof of the age, and according to their rules they had paid quite as much as they were entitled to do. It would be throwing money away to bring an action.— Mr. Aaron said the action ought to be brought if only to show up the dealings of the Society.—Mr. Edwards said after a man had paid the premiums agreed upon for over 30 years it was a mere quibble to say he had given a wrong age.—After further discussion Mr. Aaron with- drew his motion on the advice of the Clerk.
PRESENTATION TO SUPERINTENDENT NOBLETT FORMERLY OF WIDNES.

Yesterday afternoon, an interesting gathering i took place n the Court Room, of Widnes Police Station. In December last Superintendent N ob- lett was promoted to the more important County division of Bury, and a number of the tradespeople and friends met to do him honour. Although only in the Chemical centre a period of two years,Super- intendent Noblett had won the good will and the respect of all classes of the community, and in token of this feeling a number of tradesmen volun- tarily sub.:cribed towards a suitable present and Superintendent Keighley on their behalf presented him with a handsome gold hunter (chronometer) watch, suitably subscribed. In reply Superintend- ent Noblett said he had always endeavoured to perform his duty honestly and impartially, but, he felt that he had done nothing to deserve this acknowledgment. He nevertheless appreciated the feelings that had prompted it and the watch would be a reminder to him through life of his Widnes friends. (Applause.) A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the proceedings.

div.head: CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE FOR
div.p: A CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE FOR
NORTHWICH DIVISION,

At last a gentleman has been found to contest the Northwich Division against Mr. J. T. Brunner, the sitting member. For the last eighteen months an effort has been made to get a gentleman to lead the forlorn hope, but a decided "No" has been received from those who know most about the district. Mr. Hornby Lewis, of Marbury Hall,had the last refusal of the honour,but now a stranger has been found to fill the breach. The Joint Selection Committee of the North wich Division Conservative Association and the Liberal Unionist Association have decided to re- commend the Executive Committee to adopt Mr. George Whiteley, of Beech Wood, Blackburn,cotton spinner, as the Unionist candidate to oppose Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., at the next general election. Mr. Whiteley, it is stated, has expressed his willingness to contest the division, and he will be asked to ad- dress the General Committee at Northwich on the 20th inst. He will then probably be formally adopted. Mr. Whiteley is the Chairman of the Black- burn Conservative Association, and is an ex-Mayor of the borough. He is 34 years of age.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.

TELIIRSDAT.—Before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes. IMPORTANT TO PARENTS. —Eleanor Johnstone, of Lorne Villa, Froghall-lane, Warrington, who keeps a private school, sued Thomas Breakell, of Moore, who is employed on the Ship Canal for £1 165. in lieu of a term's notice of the withdrawal of a child of the defendant's who was one of the plaintiff's scholars. Mr. Unsworth (Messrs. Jenkins and Unsworth) appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. A. Browne defended. According to the prospectus of the plaintiff the year was divided into terms, and a term's notice was required before a scholar was with- drawn. This notice, it was alleged, had not been given. After hearing the evidence his Honour said he was satisfied that a distinct notice had not been given,and he, ' therefore, gave a verdict for the plaintiff .—The same plaintiff also sued T. 11. Poole, draper. Sankey-street, for a term's fees of three children in lieu of sufficient notice. Mr. Unsworth again appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Browne for the defendant. It appeared that Mrs. Poole had written to the plaintiff in August, 1891, six or seven days after the term had begun giving notice that, at the end of the term, the children would be withdrawn from the school, but this notice the plaintiff declined to accept as not having been given either before the quarter began or on the first day of the quarter. Mr. Browne submitted that the notice was sufficient, seeing that it was over seventeen weeks before the end of the term when the children were withdrawn from the school. His Honour said the plaintiff's prespeotus of terms might have been more

Iclearly drawn up, but he sympathised with those who kept a school like the plaintiff in requiring proper notice for, otherwise, how could they mike proper arrange- ments for the coming quarter. Hethought the defendant distinctly understood when the term commenced, and he gave a verdict for the plaintiff with Costs. VEHICLES IN COLLISION.—CLAIM FOR £25.—A jury was empanelled in a case in which Jonathan Finch, wholesale confectioner, Bewsey-bridge, Warrington, sued R. McDougall and Co., Limited, Renshaw-st., Liverpool, undertakers, for the sum of £25 as compensation for damages sustained in a collision of vehicles. Dr. Thomas, of Liverpool (instructed by Messrs. Jenkins and Una- worth) appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. E. Berry, of Liverpool, for the defendants. This case engaged the court for a considerable time, a strong array of wit-, nesses being called, but the facts elicited came within a limited compass. On December 22nd one of Mr. Finch's sons took out a horse and van, the van containing, it was estimated, about £l4 or £l5 worth of bottles and boxes of confectioneries, itc. The return journey was made late at night, and when coming along Liverpool. road at Sankey Bridges about half-past eleven, a collision took place between the van and a mourning coach belonging to the defendants. The coach and a hearse had been to a funeral at Davenham and were returning to Liverpool at the time when the collision took place. The van and horse were thrown over and a considerable quantity of the contents of the van were smashed and thrown over the roadway and spoiled. Defendant's son was thrown violently from the vehicle, and he was seriously cut and bruised. He stated, and his evidence was supported by a lad named Daniel Ryder who was also in the van at the time of the accident that the van was as close to its proper side of the road as it could get, and they both shouted to the defendant's drivers to keep on their own side. James Drinkwater, who lives at Sankey Bridges, and P.S. Devlin, who both saw where the van was capsized, also deposed that it was on its own side of the roadway. Drinkwater also stated that when he went up to where the crash took place he saw one of the defendant's drivers apparently looking about for his hat. He asked him to give some assistance but he declined and got on to his vehicle and drove away. Jonathan Finch, the plaintiff, gave evi- dence as to the various items of his claim. The damage to the contents of the van he reckoned to be about £7. James Heywood, wheelwright, Moore, said he was repairing the van at an estimated cost of £8; and Jacob Lawton, saddler, Sankey-street, said the repair to the harness would cost about £l.. A verdict was given for the plaintiff for LH.

div.head: REV. A. MURSELL AT WARRINGTON. SERMON ON SPURGEON.
div.p: THE REV. A. MURSELL AT WARRINGTON. SERMON ON SPURGEON.

On Thursday afternoon, the Rev. A. Mursell, of London, preached in Bold-at. Wesleyan Chapel, his subject being "In Memoriam—C. 11. Spurgeon." He said that in the second epistle of Timothy, fourth chapter, seventh verse, they read the motto which had been placed upon the casket which contained the remains of the great preacher who had been taken away—"l have fought a good fight." He re- marked that so far as thy could tell there was only one man in all the history of the world who,without any extraneous aid,had kept within the orbit of his su.,gle voice for something like 40 years an undi- minished and unbroken host of 5,000 twice each Sabbath day—of busy people in a busy time,of list- less people in a listless day,and of carping people in a carping age, and compel them to leave their busi- ness, their listlessness and quibbling behind them whilst he simply told them that it was a faithful saying, and worthy of all accepta- tion that Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners, and that one man was Charles Haddon Spurgeon who was now with God. For a success so unique and so unparalleled there must surely have been a unique characteristic to account It was not eloquence, for thousands of men had been more eloquent than he. He sought his tails- man in the truth of what he preached or what he believed to be the truth, and what he deemed to be true was the truth to him. The more directly and the more simply he could manage to tell the truth the bettar he was pleased. If a word of one syllable would do, he never used one of two, and amidst all his wealth of illustration he chose those which were the homeliest and the most direct. His very egotism, and he was in a sense egotistical,was for Christ's sake. He was showing to him (Mr. Mursell) one day a number of caricatures of himself all of which were hideous and many of them vulgarly spiteful and .unjust, and he asked Mr. Spurgeon if it did not irritate him. He replied, his face beaming with a sincerity which proved his words, and holding up a vile cartoon with horns and tail "Irritated ! What for? It is not what they write or do that hurts, it is when they cease to write or think that lam un- comfortable. A man who is worth caricaturing and abusing is worth thinking about, and when men are thinking about me they may perhaps think of my message." Message. That word sounded perfectly natural from him. It was his perfectly unqualified conviction of his personal anointing and commis- sion to one work which gave him that dogmatic and irresistable despotism over the ordinary man. He could not reason; he was convinced and that was quite enough. George Eliot, the great novelist, once heard a sermon by Mr. Spurgeon and came away with the opinion that it was the "most super- ficial grocer's back-parlour view of Christianity" she had ever heard. But he (Mr. 3lursell) called that praise and not blame. Mr. Spurgeon did not preach for great novelists but for great sinners, and the common people heard him gladly.

div.head: LECTURE ON AMERICA.
div.p: LECTURE ON AMERICA.

In the evening Mr.Mursell lectured to a large audience in Bold-st. Wesleyan schoolroom, on "America and the stranger, and how we struck each other." Mr. Tay- lor presided,and there was also on the platform the Revs. J. Gunnell and T. Ross. The lecture, which was deli- vered at a great speed, as though the lecturer was rac- ing against time, greatly interested the audience. Mr. Mursell began with his voyage across the Atlantic, and alluded in a humourous manner to his experiences of sea sickness. New York he considers to be about the worst paved city he ever saw, and this was due to its corrupt and execrable municipal government. It was, however, not a typical American city by any means, and this was due to the preponderating foreign element im- ported into the city from European countries. The elevated railroads at once struck the visitor.and a greater public convenience or a greater private outrage it was impossible to conceive. He next referred to the splendid river steamboats, the comfortable churches, and the admirably equipped hotels. As waiters, however' he greatly preferred the much-abused negro to the "free and independent" Yankee, who seemed to be far too fond of chewing tobacco and expectorating to suit Mr. Mursell's tastes. An interesting account was given of interviews whir Longfellow, Oliver Wendell Holmes and I Lloyd Garrison. In conclusion the lecturer made an eloquent peroration on the theme of " Home, sweet home," in which his allusions to England and Canada were eminently patriotic. A vote of thanks to Mr. Mursell was passed on the motion of Rev. T. Ross, seconded by Mr. T.Morris. A similar vote to the Chair- man brought the meeting to a cloae.

div.head: FUNERAL OF MR. AND MRS. YARWOOD.
div.p: FUNERAL OF MR. AND MRS. YARWOOD.

On Monday, the mortal remains of Mr. and Mrs. Thos. Yarwood, of Martinscroft, near Warrington, were interred in the burial ground attached to Run- corn Parish Church. They had both attained 73 years of age, and had been married 20 years, she being Mr. Yarwood's third v ife. Their deaths oc- curred on Thursday, within a few hours of each other. The coffins containing the remains were con- veyed by hearse to Runcorn. Behind came three b roughams,in which were the relatives, namely, Mr. and Mrs. John Alfred Yarwood (Manchester), Mr. and Mrs. Henry James Yarwood (Manchester), Mrs. A. Hleave (Appleton), Mr. and Mrs. Henry Yarwood (High Legh), Mr. and Mrs. John Yarwood (Bolling- ton), Mr. Naylor (Stockton Heath), and Mrs. Heath (Wilderspool). On the cortegereaching Delph Bridge, Halton-road, a number of Wesleyans joined, includ- ing some with whom Mr. Yarwood laboured years ago. These gentlemen included the Rev.W. Arrow- smith, Mr. J. Frith, Mr. John Pope, Mr. S. Ravens croft, Mr. Robert Norman, Mr. Thomas Cook, Mr. 0. Finlow, Mr. John Temperley, Mr. John Rutter, and Mr. J. Bazley. At the church the uaourners in- cluded Mr. S. Yarwood, of Runcorn, the youngest brother of the late Alr.Thomas Yarwood,and Messrs. F. and W. Yarwood, nephews. The Rev.Jos.Holden. senior curate at the Parish Church, officiated. Upon the coffin were a number of wreaths sent by rela- tives. The funeral arrangements were efficiently conducted by Messrs. Yarwood Bros., Albert-streets Runcorn.

WARRINGTON RAGGED SUNDAY SCI 1001; On Sunday evening at 6.30 a service was held in the above school. Mr. Owen, of Walker-street, took the chair, and also gave a suitable address. Nearly 200 were present. Sacred solos and recitations were rendered by Scholars. SatoKING CONCERT AT BtairoNwooD. A successful smoking concert was held at the Burtonwood Workingmen's Social Club, on Satur- day evening, when there was a large audience, Mr. 'Jackson, Collins Green, presiding. Songs were contributed by Messrs. J. Williams, J. liuddleston, J. Porter, and W. Beatty, and Mr. Smith, of Sutton, gave one or two recitations. Mr. J. Cunlifta ' presided at the piano,

div.head: BEFORE THE MA.GISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MA.GISTRATES.

A DISGRACEFUL COUPLE. At the Borough Police Court, on Monday, Mary Ellen Smith, Buckley-St., and Peter JohniKn, labourer, Percival's Fold, were charged with indecent conduct, al- so with assaulting Wm. Russell, on Saturday night, in Suez-st. Mr. Russell said he heard a disturbance outside his door and a woman shouting " murder." He went out and the male prisoner, and a woman he could not swear to, came into his ground. He told them they must go out, or they would be locked up. He followed than out to close the gate after them, upon which the man turned round and struck him. Witness's wife came out and the man struck her also.—They were sent- enced to a month's imprisonment with hard labour each.

div.head: DE TERMINED_ THEFT._
div.p: A DE TERMINED_ THEFT._

Thomas Murphy, factory hand, late of Stockport, but who described himself as a native of Warrington, was charged at the Borough Police Court, yesterday, with stealing, on the previous night, from the shop of Herbert Pearce, 74, Buttermarket-st., two pairs of socks, and a - quantity of wool, value 96. It appeared that about half-past 11 on Thursday night, John Plinston, cab driver, was passing near the shop and saw the prisoner hurrying up Orford-st. with some wool, Plinston gave an alarm, and the prisoner was apprehended. He had deliberately smashed the window, and taken the articles out. He was sent to prison ftfr twd months; with hard labour. A. PLATE GLASI SMASHER. At the Borough Magistrated Court, en Tuesday, Mary McLoughlin, wife of Michael McLoughlin, bricksetter, Portland-st., was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Tanner's-lane, on Monday night, and with wilfully breaking a plate glass window, value £2 15s.,at , the Three Pigeons public-house in that thoroughfare. She came into the house drunk with a can, for a pint, and the barman would not supply her, and on her refusing to go, put her out. She rushed back into the hodse screaming. He put her out again, but before he got her out, she smashed the plate glass window with the can. —The Chairman (to the prisoner) : You are rather good at window-breaking. You have managed to break four windows in your time.—She was fined £2. A THANKLESS RUFFIAN.' At the Borough magistrates' court, on Monday, John Allen, navvy, 219, Knutsford-road, was charged with being drunk and disorderlydn that road on Saturday night, also with assaulting P.C. Hollinsworth (13). The constable saw him fall in the mud in Mersey-street, and he and two men named Baxter and Ryden picked him up and took him home. There he took off his, coat and waistcoat, and struck the offieer five or six times in the face, knocking a tooth out and making his nose and mouth bleed. He also tore his cape. Baxter and Ryden stood at the door and they assisted the constable, Baxter being assaulted in the scale. A bus was stopped, and some passengers gave up theirseats to allow the prisoner to be taken in it to the police Stetion.—lie was fined 40e. and costs; and Baxter and Ryden were compli- mented by the Chairman on their conduct. A JUVENILE PICKPOCKET. At the Borough Police Court, on Monday merning, Theresa Weave, aged 11, and Mary Gleave, fustian cutter, aged 16, daughters of Thomas Gleave, 8 Jones's buildings, Winwick road, were charged with stealing a purse containing £1 2s. from Mrs. Mary Myles, wife of Harry Myles, the previous afternoon. There was a funeral from Jones's buildings, and Mrs. Myles,who had an infant in her arms, was standing looking on, when the younger prisoner took the purse out of her pocket, at the instigation of the elder girl. Mrs. Myles did not discover her loss until she returned to her house, and then information was given to the police by her husband. H.S. Monaghan traced the theft to the prisoners, and apprehended then. They admitted their guilt, and a conviction was recorded against Theresa, Mary be- ing ordered to be detained in the cells till six o'clock on Tuesday evening;

A TIIIHVISM CUSTOMER. As the Warrington borough police court, on *ednes- day John Lydon, an Irish ship canal labourer, who has been lodging at No. 4, Dutton street, was charged with stealing 31b of potatoes the property of Ellen Smith, provision dealer,l26 Nersev street. He went in the shop and asked for 3W of .potatoes and put thern into his pockets, s.nd when.,the girl who kiipplied hitn with them asked him to pay, used disgraceful language to her, and walked out without paying. 'The girl went to the police station, and he was apprehended—The Chief Constable said if there had been a man about the place the prisoner would not have done this. If there was a woman alone in a shop it was a very different matter ; these navvies wanted teaching a lesson different from this.—The prisoner, who said he was drunk at the. time, was sentenced to a month's imprisonment with hard labour.
TELF:vr OF TOOLS.

At the Wartington Borough Magistrates' Court, on Tuesday morning, Lewis Jones' joiner, of No. 3, Ship- yard, formerly of Liverpool, and lately employed by William Walter Dobson,cabinetinaker,Buttermarket- st., was charged with stealing, some time between the 25th ult. and the Bth inst., two planes, a spring balance, some chisels, &c., value 293., the property of Mr.Dobson. On Monday morning, the prosecutor having missed the articles,sent for the prisoner, and accused him of having stolen the articles. He admitted his guilt, and pro- duced pawn tickets for several tools pledged by him. The police were informed, and P.C. Phillips took him into custody. The constable found that not only had the tools been pledged, but other articles had been sold to Mrs. Leslie, Mersey-et —P.C. Phillips : The prisoner told me he was in drink and he had pledged the things to get drink.—The Chiet Constable said the prisoker lived in a warm shoo for drink—Ship-yard.—Jones was sent to prison for a month with hard labour.

- A finw IN A TANTARD. At the borough police court, yesterday,William Ward' labourer, 3, Admiral-street, and Joseph Ward, labourer, 41, School Brow, both employed by Mr. J. El. Fleming, tanner, were charged with. being drunk and disorderly the previous morning. William was also charged with assaulting Mr. J. H. Fleming, pin., and Daniel Parkes, a labourer employed in the tanyar,d, and both men were charged with assaulting P.C. s Purner and Phillips. It appeared from the evidence that about 10 o'clock in the morning William Ward came to the yard drunk and wanted to go out with the horse,but, as he was not fit to drive, Mr. Fleming, jun., would not allow him to go. He kept hold of the horse, and ?M!. Fleming got another man to take it, hut William Ward, would not let him do so. Mr. Fleming then sent for a policeman and P.C. Turner came, and afterwards P.C. Phillips. Mr. Fleming tried to put the man out of the yard. but he would not go, and he kicked him and threatened him. He also assaulted David Parkes who came to assist Mr. Fleming. P.C. Turner tried to put him out, and he picked up a weight from a weigh- ing machine and struck him with it knoc king his hel- met off. Be also hit the constable. Phillips took the weight from him,and he was put out of the yard. Joseph then came up and ran at Turner and Phillips and kicked them. Joseph got away, but they took William to the station, he striking them all the way; and afterward ap- prehended Joseph. It WAS stated that the weight with which William struck Turner would have killed him • hut for his helmet.-7-Ths Chairman: There might have been murder committed in this case.—William. denied using the weight, and said the constable had used him badly and thrown a bucket of water over him.—He was sent to prison for two months, and :his brother for 14 days, both with bard labour.

and Alderman Wright. - DRUNK IN CHARGH OF A lloasz.—James Wilkinson, drunk in charge of a horse and cart in Knutsford-road, the previous afternoon, a constable stating that the man was so drunk and unmanageable that he had to be held down in the cart, was tined 3.05. and 3s. 6d. and costs.,

THIIRSDAY.—Before Major Pickmere (chairman), Alder- men Sutton and Chandley, Councillor James Fair- dough, and Captain Ridgway. NON-EDUCATION OF CHILDREN.—At the instance of Mr. G. Evans, butcher, New-road, was charged with not sending his children to school. It appearing in this case that the fault was on the part of the mother, the Chairman asked Mr. Riley if there was no means of sending the wife to prison if the husband would not pay the fine.—Mr. Riley said there was not.—The Chairman : If we could only get the law altered that way what a blessing it would be !- -Alderman Sutton (to Mr. Riley) : Supposing you had a wife who acted in that manner what would you do ? Mr. Riley : I should try to conquer—to cure her.—The Chairman : " A woman, a dog, and a walnut tree, the more you beat them the better they'll be ' they say. The worst of it is the law intervenes sometimes, but it is very hard that the husband should be punished where the wife is at fault.—The defendant was fined Vb.—John Goddard, Beswick-st.. ss.—John Mannion, labourer Ashton's-Vard, ss.—Thos. FOOTBALL.

.„a Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that eporte of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.
RUGBY.
WARRINGTON v. WIDNES "A "—Played at Warrington. Warrington had the best of the play all through and ended in winning by 2-1-5 to 0-0-2.
RUNCORN v. TUEBROOK.

At Runcorn on Saturday Runcorn team was seven of the usual players short and Tuebrook had not their best team. A capital open game was witnessed. The Tue- brook men led off with a try by Bleasdale, and after this Runcorn assumed the attack. Pendlebury, Hollings- worth, and Gayter scored for Runcorn. Dolan, Massey, Lee,and Davies were the pick of a sharp lot of forwards, and in addition to May, Hollingsworth, Robinson, and Pendlebury played a dashing game behind the scrim- mage. May's display at centre was very fine, and he dropped a splendid goal in second half. The Tuebrook men played a nice open game, and passed well, but the forwards ought to pack better and thus give their half backs a chance of obtaining the ball. Ellains as centre was decidedly weak, but Pearson and Bailey were very active. Runcorn ran out winners by 13 points to Toe- brook two points. WARRINGTON V. WIDNES.

What with International and County matches, the football world on Saturday was fully engaged. Out- side the aforementioned games the return engagement between Warrington and Widnes was first in importance, and despite the counter-attractions at Whalley Range and Birkenhead, the gate at Lowerhouse-lane ground, Whines, must have numbered considerably over 5,000. The first contest had resulted in a defeat of the Widnes- ians, and, with the homesters on the present occasion fully bent on reversing the first result, everything pointed to a capital contest. The Warringtonians lacked the service of such an able trio as John Bate, Nevins, and Jolley, the latter being down with the influenza. Nearly 1,000 Warrington enthusiasts journeyed to Wid- nes to witness the match. Winning the toss, the home- sters took advantage of the light breeze, and Turner's kick being luckily got away by Barber, Heesom was at once to the front with a short run to centre, where play raged for a time. A spell of kicking gave no material advantage to either team, but some capital play by the Widnes forwards placed the Warrington goal in jeopardy. The homesters main- tained their advantage, and despite a gallant attempt to clear by Bate, the Widnes front rank again bore down with remarkable energy. A free kick granted to each side found play at the visiting quarter flag, and, Boscow was applauded for .getting the oval away when severely pressed. Barber responded in fine style, and the effort being supplemented by Wright and Drummond, the latter had hard lines when nearly all opposition had been cleared. Webster, Heesom, Evans, and Boscow defended their charge in fine style, but a short kick by Brennan saw Bescow held under the posts. With Buckley, Turner, and Berry at the head of affairs, the Warringtonians rushed the oval out of danger, and Hartles being foiled by Bate the Widnes goal was for the first time threatened. Widnes once more returned to the attack by the aid of Peters, and a fine drop by Bar- ber sent the oval dead. Widnes still assumed the ag- gressive, and a fine chance was missed when Hewitt passed forward a yard from the line. Boscow again made his mark under difficulties, but only a few yards was gained, and although Turner, Berry, Davies, and Teare dribbled consecutively, the vigorous play of the home forwards nullified all Warrington's efforts to change the scene of action. Evans tackled Peters grandly on one occasion, whilst the next moment Buckley rushed down the open,reaching the half-way flag. Widnes were again penalized, but the kick acted as little relief for Warrington, for the determined play of the homesters soon landed the oval again on their opponents' line. Evans now made his mark, but Wright nullified the effort by a short run, being hauled down by Heesom. From the pack on the line Bate essayed to clear, but finding his way blocked tried to punt, but disaster attended the effort, for the kick was charged down, and Whelan was enabled to score a somewhat easy try. Barber placing a neat goal. The play still continued in favour of Widnes, and despite the brilliant endeavours of Ashton, Turner, Bandies, Webster, and Bate, no impression could be made on the Widnes defence. Some hot scrimmages ensued opposite the Warrington posts, but a grant piece of combination by Bate, Heesom, Webster, and Evaes,took play beyond the half-way flag. Another piece of 'combination by Lawless, Bate and Evans forced the game oa the line, and although the home forwards milled the oval partially' out of dan- ger, Boscow, with a judicious kick, gave his side the upper hand. Berry and Donohue were too quick for Battles on one occasion, but Wright with tricky play soon had the oval at centre field,where Brennan received from Drummond, and, running stronglyelinally passed to Forster, who managed to get over after a scrambling effort, Barber failing at the place. With seven points to the bad, the drop-out was effected, and Turner and Davies, with seperate efforts, landed the game at the Widnes end. A concerted movement between Berry, Buckley, and Team was followed by Brennan being splendidly tackled by Heesom. Widnes now made a fly- ing excursion to the Warrington end, but Ashton and Donohue had the oval back at their opponents' end in douole-quick time, and Hartles being at fault, the home- sters' defence was severely harassed. A spell of passing by Bate and Heesom saw the latter transferring very low to Webster, with the consequence that a splendid oppor- tunity was missed. Barber relieved slightly,whilst a punt across to Evans saw that player failing to get up in time to make use of the chance proffered. Warrington maintained their position, and after Boscow had res- ponded gallantly to a kick by Peters. Webster tried a shot at goal without success. The next minute, how- ever, saw Bate, Heesom, and Webster passing grandly, and the latter got over near the corner flag. Turner failed at the difficult place. Flay WAS on the Widnes line when half time was called with the score—Widnes, 1-1-1 ; Warrington, 0-1-0. On resuming, Bate was the . first to show up with a brilliant run along the popular side, and several efforts by the Warrington forwards were deserving of substantial results. Donohue got in from a brilliant piece of play by Webster, but the appeal was overruled. Barber next got clear, but found. a _ .

match in Webster, for half-a-d-ozeri strides sufficed for the capture of the Widnesian. The oval was soon on the home lines again, and Webster punted to Ferster (who had replaced Hartles at back). From some loose play Davies almost landed a goal from a flying kick. After some even play, Bate got clear from a scrim- mage opposite the stand, and ran finely along touch. being hauled down when on the verge of scoring. Warrington assumed the aggressive right up to the close of hostilities, but failed to draw level, and when the whistle sounded, the scores read—Widnes, 1-1-2 ; Warrington, 0-1-3. Teams :—Warrington : 13oscow, back ; Evans, Haesom, and Webster, three-quarterbacks; James Bate and Lawless, half backs ; Ashton, Turner, Bandies, Berry, Thorniley, Donohue, Davies, Teare, and Buckley, forwards. Widnes : Rattles, back ; Barber, Brennan, and Peters, three-quarter backs ; Drummond and Wright, half-backs; Emery, Forster, Farmer, Hewitt, Whelan, Gordon, Lyons, Ridgway, and John- son; forwards.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.

FOOTRALL.—RUGBY. Englishmen are not likely to find much comfort from the display of their representatives at Whalle,y Range on Saturday last. Instead Of disposing of Ireland with something very considerable in band, as was generally expected, they gave their supporters a bad time of it, and it was not until the game was well advanced that they gained the upper hand. The alterations in the English team that conquered Wales were supposed to have strengthened it, and as Ireland were disappointed by several of the selected players failing to keen their , appointments everything seemed to point to a certain victory for the home side. Hence few were prepared for such a stiff contest. The Irishmen played up in a style that for a long time boded ill for their antagonists, but combination told its tale in the end and England finished up on the right side.

The attendance was very gratifying, and showed what a strong hold international football has in the affections of the British public. The arrangements were in every way satisfactory, and on looking round at the magnificent assemblage Messrs. M`Laren and Payne and their colleagues must have felt rewarded for -their labours. The afternoon was very favourable, and the ground appeared to be in decent order.

Anyone who looked for a runaway exhibition must have been quickly undeceived, as the Iristunen threw such an amount of energy into their work as to make it clear that they were really formidable opponents. The forwards were in earnest, and carried the packs re• peatedly, whilst they were also very quick and eager when the ball came in the loose. Indeed the forward department on the English side did not compare at all well, and it was mainly owing to this that there was no score up to the interval. The backs had on several occa- sions all they could do to keep out the Irishmen, who were well pleased with themselves on crossing over.
The same kind of thing went on until well into the second half, and the followers of the English team were
