div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 13, 1892. THE LATE MR. SPURGEON.
div.p: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 13, 1892. THE LATE MR. SPURGEON.

rapidly becoming despondent as to the issue. jzlad not Bullough smartly charged down that free kick there is no telling what might have happened, as the ball was apparently making straight for goal. The great efforts of the visitors now began to tell on them, whereas their antagonists were playing somewhat better together, and when Woods placed a splendid goal from Evershed'e try anxiety was set at rest. Evershed had also a good deal to do with the try scored by Percival, but in this ease the place was not successful, and when all was over Eagland were victorious by seven points to none.

There were weak places in the English team without a doubt that will need seeing to in view of the all-import- ant struggle with Scotland. This was chiefly noticeable among the forwards, some of whom did not take at all kindly to the scrimmages. It was this defect that cost us the match with Scotland last year, as feeble forward play quite upset the backs.

The best feature in the play of the Irishmen was their tackling. Everyone of them cams off with credit in this line,and it was owing to this fact that there was not a really good run by an Englishman all the afternoon. Peel was an excellent full back, and Gardiner and Dun- lop were untiring at three-quarters. One run by Gardiner in the second half came in for rounds of cheer- ing. Thornhill was rather better than Tuke at half hick, but neither of them can be termed high class. The forwards deserve the warmest praise. It was most refreshing to see them go into the scrimmages with such vigour, Lefanu, O'Connor, Hooke, and Walsh sett- ing their comrades a brilliant example that they very readily followed. They received, plenty of encourage- ment from the big crowd, who were most impartial in their plaudits.

So far as one can judge, Scotland's boasted superior- ity this season exists only on paper. They intended making short work of Wales, but the most they could do with them was te beat them by a goal and a try to a try. This advantage was secured prior to the inter- val, after which the defence of both sides was kept in- tact. There were only three changes in last year's Scotch team, whereas only three of last season's Welsh ' players now did duty. The latter were stronger than when they left England, the appearance of the brothers James at half back being an undoubted gain.

As Cheshire could not see their way to altering the date of their fixture with Yorkshire, the latter sent a very scratchy team to Birkenhead, and thus sustained their first reverse of the season. Any other result would have been lowering to the dignity of the Cestrians, who would much have preferred to have met the full strength of the champion county. Blackburn, the Cleckheaton back, is blamed for the defeat, as he ought to have stopped Jones when he scored the winning point. Vic- tory was represented by 13 points to 12. The place kicking of Cheshire was capable of much improvement.

Manchester and Swinton each postponed their engage- ments in view of the international at Whalley Range. Salford took on Burton-on-Trent, and bad not much difficulty in overcoming their visitors. Broughton had an easy prey in Owen's College, the latter having their lines invaded on no fewer than six occasions. Manches- ter Rangers finished up a try in front of Dukinfield, but the last-named were minus Haslam, their trusty full back. Liverpool went down at Bradford and Wigan at Halifax. Wigan find it no easy matter to fill Ander- ton's place. About the heaviest score of the afternoon was that of Brighouse Rangers against Hull—five pals and three tries to a try : but it was nearly equalled by Cambridge University at Richmond.

The following players have been chosen to represeat Lancashire in the match against the Midland Counties at Whalley Range to-day (Saturday) :—T. Coop (Leigh), back; J. Valentine (Swinton), J. B. Stork (Liverpool), and W. ACCutcheon (Oldham), three-quarter backs ;J. T. Bate (Warrington), and W. Cross (St. Helens), half backs ; E. Bullough (Wigan), R. P. Wilson (Liverpool Old Boys), T. Craven (Salford), T. Kent (Salford), T. Bothwell (Swinton), S. R. Wilson (Liverpool), E. W. Bullen (Liverpool Old Boys), A. Ashworth (Oldham),and J. Pyke (St. Helens Recreation), forwards.
MEMORIAL SERVICES.

Memorial services were held on Wednesday for the late Mr. Spurgeon in the Metropolitan Tabernacle. The coffin containing the body rested amongst foliage and flowers in view of the congregation. Long before the hour fixed for the first memorial ser- vice the building was filled. The children of Stockwell Orphanage, dressed in mourning, sang hymns .prior to the commeacernent of the service. The Rev. James Spurgeon presided, and addresses were delivered by Dr. Angus, Dr. Pierson, the Rev. J. Flarrald, and several deacons. The service throughout was of a most impres- sive character,and the congregation were deeply affected. At the afternoon service, the Tabernacle was filled with ministers and students. Dr. Pierson and the Rev. D.Davies, of Brighton,offered prayers ; and Dr. M‘Laren delivered an impressive address. rife Rev. Canon Fleming, a personal friend of Mr. Spurgeon, and who attended as honorary secretary of the Religious Tract Society, followed with an eloquent eulogium on the de- parted pastor. The service was very impressive, and the singing of the hymns by the 6,000 men in the build- ing was a thing almost unique. The following telegram from Mrs. Spurgeon was read :—" Mentone. My heart bleeds with yours, but our beloved's joy is full. We shall see him again, and our hearts shall rejoice. Death shall be swallowed up in victory, and the Lord God will wipe the tears from all faces."

THE FUNERAL.—IMPRESSIVE SERVICE. Signs of mourning in South London on Thursday were of a very widespread character. Most of the lead- ing tradespeople closed their shops for the day,and those places of business that were open had either their blinds drawn or shutters up. With the opening of the doors of the Tabernacle at 10 a.m. the building rapidly filled. The floor and lower galleries were thronged with a congregation of about 6,000 persons. 'Agreeably to the request of the deacons that cheques should be sent instead of wreaths, several hundreds of pounds have been received for the Pastors College and Orphan- age, among them being four for £lOO. At 11 a.m. on the upper platferm supporting Dr. Pierson and other , ministers, were the Rev. C. Spurgeon and Mrs. C. Spurgeon, Dr. Allot], the Mayor, Town Clerk, and sev- eral aldermen of Croydon, and Messrs. Colman, Waddy, and Hoyle, members of Parliament. Over 60 deputa- tions were present, as also were the children from the Stockwell Orphanage. The service began by the sing- ing of the hymn, " Servant of God, well done." The hymn was followed by a prayer from Mr. Harrold, the [deceased's secretary. Another hymn " The Sands of Time are Sinking," the last hymn given out by the de- ceased pastor, followed, and then Dr. Pierson delivered an address in which he compared Mr. Spurgeon to Charles Wesley. At the •close of the service a proces- sion was formed at the Tabernacle, and the remains of the deceased were conveyed by the Brixton-rd., to Nor- ' wood Cemetery. The cortege was preceded by three ' mounted constables. Upon the coffin was the open Bible, and on the sides of the open hearse was the text in white lettering, "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course." The whole route was lined with spectators, and the bells of St. Mary's, Newington, and St. Mark's, Kennington, were tolled, whilst the children of Stockwell Orphanage occupied a raised platform at the entrance of the institution as the procession passed. The Biskop of Rochester was in one of the mourning coaches which entered the ground. The service was conducted by the Rev. Archibald Brown, who, after the cemmital of the body to the ground, delivered a short address, during which the vast audience were visibly affected. The Bishop of Rochester, pronounced the Benediction. A solemn memorial service was held in Myrtle-st. Baptist Chapel, Liverpool, and eulogies on the deceased were delivered by Mr. W. P. Lockhart, the Rev. Charles. Garrett, and the Rev. Grantley C. Martin. A number of other local ' clergymen took part in the more strictly devotional parts of the service.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

Sunderland made no mistake on their second visit to Accrington. Although still on the heavy side,the ground was more to their liking, and they beat the Reds hand- somely by three goals to one in the F.A. competition. They are thus qualified to meet Stoke in the third round of ties, which are down for dispcsal on Saturday next. There should be several contests of more than passing interest. The game between Wolverhampton and Aston Villa is sure to be of a fierce description, as the two are stubborn cup fighters. West Bromwich Albion ought to accmnt for Sheffield Wednesday, and Notts Forest are pretty sanguine about their tie with Preston North End. The Forest have an unbeaten certificate so far as their own ground is concerned this season.

The Lancashire Cup ties came out in acc.)rdance with public form except in two instances. These were the fixtures at Darwen and Newton Heath. North End have such an infinitely better record than Darwen that they were regarded as certain winners, but they failed most unaccountably, and were knocked out of the corn- petition by the Barley Bank team for the second year in succession. They played poor football, and were de- servedly beaten. It was the same tale at Newton Heath. Bury were very smart all round, and fairly won their way into the second round. The Heathens sadly disappointed their admirers.

div.head: SCHOONER SUNK AND THREE LIVES
div.p: SCHOONER SUNK AND THREE LIVES

LOST. A Lloyd's Cardiff telegram says it is reported that the Cardiff steamer Earl of Dumfries ran into and sank the Bristol schooner Railway, off Bull Point on Wednesday morning. Two men and a boy were drowned, and the captain and a boy were rescued.

div.head: CARDINAL AIANNING'S SUCCESSOR.
div.p: CARDINAL AIANNING'S SUCCESSOR.

The Daily Telegraph " states that if the Bishop of Salford is appointed Cardinal Manning's successor, the second archiepiscopal see will probablv be fixed at Liverpool, and that Dr. O'Reilly will receive the title of " Primate of England." In the event of an " outsider " being appointed to Westminster, however, the Bishop of Salford would be raised to archiepiscopal rank in prefer- ence to the Bishop of Liverpool

div.head: TERRIBLE DOUBLE TRIGEDY IN LIVE RPOOL.
div.p: TERRIBLE DOUBLE TRIGEDY IN LIVE RPOOL.

The Feathers Hotel, C!ayton Square, Liverpool, was the scene of a terrible tragedy on Thursday night. Harry Thompson, a member of a firm of provision mer- chants, shot a barmaid named Emily Gillibrand with a revolver and then used the weapon upon himself. The man died on the spot, but it is expected that the young woman,who has a bullet wound in her head,will recover. For some time Mr. Thompson, in spite of-the fact that he was a married, man and ha several children residing at Waterloo, where his abode was,is known to have been smitten by the attractions of Miss Gillibrand, and it is said that a naonth ago he addressed a letter to her, stat- ing that unless his devotion be requited something of a lerrible nature would ensue.

div.head: COAL CRISIS.-MINERS' CONFERENCE.
div.p: THE COAL CRISIS.-MINERS' CONFERENCE.

A Conference to which all the mining districts were invited to send representatives was opened in Man- chester on Thursday, under the presidency of Mr. S. Woods. The purpose was to consider the present crisis in the coal trade, and to decide upon a uniform icheme of joint action by the miners of the United Kingdom with a view to stop the system "of selling surplus coal at unprofitable prices, which is the chief cause of the reductions in miners' wages." Over 175,000 financial members of the Minors' Pecleration were represented. The business transacted on lb.ursday was of a prelimin- ary character. It was reported that the miners of Dur- ham, Northumberland, South Wales. and all the districts of Scotland had been specially invited to send represen- tatives to the Conference, but had not done so.

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

Speaking at a meeting of his constituents at Bury on Wednesday night, Sir Henry James again raised the religious cry in regard to the policy of Home Rule for Ireland. Lloyd's agent at Monte Video states that the natives have commenced to plunder the British barque Crown of Italy, previously reported lost off Sart Diego. The fate of the crew is unknown. _ . „

„. Lord Carrington spoke at Liverpool on Wednesday night on the Flume Rule question, arguing that the Em- pire would be saved not, ny insisting on centralised authority, but by giving self-government to all its parts. A Bucharest newspaper reports a dreadful occurrence on the express train from Bucharest to Brails. A first- class sleeping carriage caught fire, and, the doors being locked, eighteen of the twenty occupants were either fatally burned or suffocated. The death is announced at Milton Green, Cheshire, of Win. Penny, supposen to he between 104 and 105 years of age. Penny had in his possession a certificate of baptism, dated 99 years back, and the old man stated that he perfectly remembered walking to church for the ceremony when five years of age. At the Old Bailey, on Thursday, the trial of Mr. Hast- ings, M.P., was adjourned till next sessions. The adjournment was granted at the request of Mr. Lyttle- ton, who said there were certain matters which., in the interests of the defendant, required fuller investigation than had been possible since the committal. Mr. Jenkins gave evidence before the Labour Com- mission on Wednesday, on behalf of the Monmouth- shire and South Wales Coalowners' Association_ He stated that an eight hours day from bank to bank would mean only five and a half hours' actual work, which would twilit in the.closiug of sornepines.

div.head: LOCAL SERMONS. WARRIISGTON.
div.p: LOCAL SERMONS. WARRIISGTON.

At Wycliffe Church, on Sunday evening, the Rev. J. Yonge, preached with special reference to the death of Mr. Spurgeon. The text was 2 Timothy, iv. 7, "I have fought a good tight: I have finished my course ; I have kept the faith." These words, ob- served this speaker, were said to have been the last text of Scripture that Mr. Spurgeon repeated, when in almost immediate prospect of death. The recent past had seen some of these front rank men pass away,and they had even been admitted to the know- ledge of some of their latest and dying experiences. He could not recall a recent case in which ehe departing soldier of Christ had fatten asleep with those grand words of the text on his lips. 'they only became a great and victorious Christian. They were words of achieve- ment, and could not be uttered by any but a real and successful life. It was a remarkable tribute to the worth of the man, and the success of his ministry, that all ranks, parties, and churches united to pay him honour. The testimony was most unique, when it was remem- bered that Spurgeon was a dissenting minister, with no academic training or distinction. " C. H. Spurgeon, the man and his work," was the subject of the sermon delivered in St. John's Presbyterian Church, on Sunday evening, by the Rev. J. Warnock. The preacher said he wished that evening to draw the attention of his congregation to some of the lessons to be learned from the life and labour of the late Mr. Spur- geon. He occupied a large place in the Christian life,not only of England, but of all English-speaking people. His place as a minister of the gospel was altogether unique. Among all the preachers of the century he occupied the foremost place, and no preacher of modern times could speak to the multitude and move them as he did. The preacher was sure that generous minds in all churches would acknowledge his to be an irreparable loss to com- mon Christianity. They, as Presbyterians, had special reason to cherish his memory, for without being one of themselves, his friendship for the Reformed Churches holding tho Presbyterian system had ever been of the warmest kind. It was,perhaps,a, fitting climax to all this that his pulpit at the Metropolitan Tabernacle was dur- ing his last illness occupied by a Presbyterian minister, and that at the funeral service held in the little Presby- terian Church at Mentone, Where he died, were two resbyterian ministers, along with representatives from other churches. To hew many people, burdened with sins, sorrows, and cares, Mr. Spurgeon's ministrations had been blessed, the great day alone would declare. it mighht be said of him, as was said of . his Master, that the common people heard him gladly. The marvellous compass and musical cadence of his voice, the firmness with which he held what he believed to be the truth,the

genuine honesty and transparency of his character—these all served to render his an acceptable ministry. They probably did not err who saw in him a strong resemb- lance to the late John Bright, alike in the character of the I man and in the style of his oratory. Both were men of , great fluency of speech, and fond of plain, pithy,hornely : words, whose meaning every one could understand. I Both were men of strong wills, immovable as the rock in standing up for what they believed to be right. Both likewise were men of a genial sunny temperament, not , ntiurblly given to look at the dark side of things. People ,ometimes forgot that aspect of Mr. Spurgeon's character, o.ving to the attitude which he assumed towards many of his brethren during the past few years lout that was to allow a temporary estrangement to; eclipse the record of his whole life. On Suaday evening the Rev. J. W. Varley, preached in the Baptist Chapel, Latchford, in reference to the late C. H. Spurgeon, a very impressive sermon, to an atten- tive and large congregation, from the words, " And there arose not a prophet since in Israel like unto Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face." Dent. 34.10. The reading desk was draped in black. The pastor, after referring to Moses being leader of the Israelites,said Mr. Spurgeon was leader of the Baptists. Atter giving a short description of his life, and some of his works,the pastor said he thought the Lord would appoint some other person to carry on the great work which Mr. Spur- geon had been doing. At the close of the service Mr. W. T. Wilkinson played the Dead March in" Saul." RUNCORN. In several of the Nonconformist chapels of Runcorn, on Sunday, references were made to the death of Mr. Spurgeon, the great Baptist preacher. At St. Paul's Wesleyan Chapel, the Rev. J. Hanby, in the course of an eloquent tribute said " Speaking to the best of our knowledge, he wrote more books,edited more literature, preached more sermons, comforted more Christians, in- spired more preachers, perhaps saved more souls than any man living. He will continue to teach by his books to enthrall by his sermons, and to preach by those who have been raised from a death of sin to a life of right- eousness by his ministry." The Rev. J. Martin, pastor of the Methodist Free Churches of Runcorn and Widnes, made appropriate references to the death at both places, He described Mr. Spurgeon as the greatest preacher the world had ever seen, and said his removal was the greatest loss the world had sustained for a considerable period. Preaching at St. John's Presbyterian Church, the Rev. J. Pultord Williams said of late we had heard much of the death of maay notables of our land, chief amongst whom was the Prince, whose death was associated with circumstances of a painful character; but the Church militant suffered little from such changes. Princes and lords were but the breath of kings, but in the death of Spurgeon—he was too great for the limitation Mr.—the cause of God was reduced in strength; for it had lost an advocate that had done more than any other man of the ago to spread the knowledge of true and undefiled religion. Through the media of his wondrous voice and ever ready pen, he spoke to mankind at large—his audience was the world. At Widnes reference was also made from the various pulpits to the sad event. In the evening a memorial service was held in Milton Congregational Church. and the Rev. R. G. Hughes preached an appropriate sermon and described Mr. Spurgeon's death as a national lo.ss.
The British schooner Patriot has been towed into Bos- ton after capsizing, five of her crew having been drowned,
The prisoners Ditchfield, Battolla, Deakin, Westley, Galles, and Charles, were again remanded by the 'al- salt magistrates on Tuesday on a charge of complicity in an alleged Anarchist plot,

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held at the Town Hall, Widnes, on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. Gossage presided, and there were also present Messrs. B. Brown, R. Cooke, J. Midwood, Beech, H. S. Timmins, J. Houghton, "J. Taylor, F. Heyes, J. Tilley, J. Carroll, H. S. Oppenheim (clerk), and other officers.

div.head: THE-LATE DUKE OF CLARENCE.
div.p: THE-LATE DUKE OF CLARENCE.

The Chairman, having remarked that that was the first meeting of that Board since the death of the Duke of Clarence; Moved a vote of sympathy with the Royal Family.—This was seconded by Mr. Browne, and agreed to.

div.head: UNEMPLOYED.
div.p: THE UNEMPLOYED.

The Clerk read a communication he had received from Mr. Mann, clerk to the Prescot Board of Guardians,with reference to giving work to the unemployed. The Clerk added that at the time the snow was on the ground the Board did engage extra men, who would otherwise have been unemployed.

div.head: PROPOSED VEHICULAR BRIDGE.
div.p: THE PROPOSED VEHICULAR BRIDGE.

The Chairman,referring to the subject of the proposed vehicular bridge connecting Runcorn and Widnes, said that he had received a private letter from Mr. George Deacon, the engineer for the Vyrnwy scheme, suggest- ing that it would be quite possible, and perhaps better. to have a tunnel under the Mersey, rather than a bridge over it. The communication was simply a personal one. Mr. Brown thought that Mr. Deacon's experience did not seem to be very encouraging.—The Chairman said the public, of course, did not quite know all that took place in regard to that matter. The shield now in use by Mr. Deacon was making remarkable progress. The following letter from Sir Douglas Fox, engineer, who was some time ago consulted as to the feasibility and cost of erecting the bridge over the Mersey at the point ,in question, was then read by the cleilt :—" I observe that Mr. Deacon has written suggesting atunnel, in place of a bridge, at this point. If you desire it, I will prepare camparative estimates, but I may at once give my opinion that a bridge will be found, in every ease, both more economical and more convenient, free from the uncertainties and risks inseparable from tunnelling under the bed of an important tidal river, with such strata as are found between Widnes and Runcorn. The approaches adapt themselves far more easily to a high level bridge than to constructing a tunnel,and for horse, carriage, and passenger traffic transit in the open air is decidedly preferable where, as in this case, it can be readily attained."—The subject then dropped.

div.head: GAS AND 'WATER COMMITTEE.
div.p: GAS AND 'WATER COMMITTEE.

The minutes of the above-named Committee contained the following items :—Gas testings :—Report of tests on the 14th, and 25th inst., read : Illuminating power, 18.66 and 20.64 candles. Free from sulphuretted hydrogen. Shooting rights, Pex Hill :—Tenders sub- mitted and considered. Recommended that the Clerk negociate with Mr. Bretherton fora lease of the shooting rights for a term of not exceeding 5 years. Netherley Extension :—Recommended that the tender of Joshua Renshaw and Sons for the erection of New Engine House &c., at Netherley for the sum of £1,530 be accepted. Recommended that the tender of Messrs. Hathurn, Davey, and Co. (274) for well room floor plates and. girders be accepted. The engineer, in his report, referred to the flood at the gas works, on the 19th and 20th January, 1892. He said that owing to the combined thaw of snow, and heavy rain Bower's Brook was again flooded on the 19th ult. The Water commenced backing up the gullies into the yard at 9 30 a.m. and continued rising until 1031) p.m., and remained stationary until 2 a.m on the 20th when it began to recede; the greatest height reached was 4 inches above the flood line of November, 1886, and 16i inches below that of November, 1890. During the early part of the day the water, by means of dams, was kept to the top end of the yard, and little damage was done, but at about 2 p.m. it began to come in from the top end of Earle-st. with great force, flooding and rendering useless both gasholders in its course, and afterwards covering the whole of the yard to the depth stated. The difficulty with the gasholders was anticipated, and they were shut off, the make of gas in the meantime being seen to and the supply obtained from Ditton. Great difficulty was experienced in keeping the mains and • syphons clear, particularly when the water was at itS greatest height. At 936 p.m. the connecting boxes at the bottoms of the condenser tubes were completely sub- merged, and gas making had for a time to be suspended, but it was afterwards found that by keeping this appa- ratus under a constant back pressure the water in the boxes was forced down sufficiently to enable the gas to just bubble through, and this, with no small amount of difficulty and risk, was done until the water receded. Six producer furnaces, which were at the time working in No. 1 retort house, were partly extinguished, the fur- naces and flues suffering considerable damage, and the heats of the retorts being greatly reduced. The supply of gas to the town was not interrupted excepting that the usual pressure was not maintained, owing to the high town governor—which would have been the first to be flooded—being shut off, and the whole of the supply having to be taken through the low town gover- nor. That the town was not plunged into darkness was due first to our having a little time, as the water rose during the day, to get everything in readiness for the worst, and further to the water stopping at the point it did, for had it risen a few inches higher, the supply,not- withstanding our every effort to keep it going, would have been stopped. The estimated damage to furnaces, steam boiler fires, and stores, also loss of sulphate of ammoniacal liquor, coke, gas, and extra wages incurred is £22s.—Recommended that an account be rendered to the United Alkali Co., Limited, of the damage sustained at the gas works in consequence of the flooding of the brook, and that they be asked for payment thereof. Recommended that the salary of Ms. Fred Thorpe, assistant gas manager, be advanced from £9O to £llO per annum.—Mr. Brown moved the confirmation of the minutes, and referred to the damage done by the flood- ing of the gas works.—Mr. Midwood asked if others had had the same opportunity of tendering for the shooting at Fax Hill as Mr. 13retherton, and he also wished to

know the terms upon which it was based.—Mr. Beech said it was thougnt that as the game all round Pax Hill belonged to Mr. Bretherton it was only fair that he should have the right of shooting there.—Mr. Brown also mentioned the sum at which the shooting rights were to be let, and which Mr. Midwood considered satisfactory. The minutes were then confirmed. iIIGITIVAYS COMMITTEE.

The Committee's minutes were confirmed on the motion of Mr. Taylor. They stated that plans of new schools in Widnes-rd., and of 22 houses in Denton-st., for Edwin Woods, were disapproved. lIMILLTH COMMITTEE. In this Committee's minutes it was stated that the birth-rate had been equal to 3257 per ,1,600, and the death-rate to 2012,. He added, " I am pleased to state that we have been tolerably free from bad cases of in- fectious disease this month. There have been numer- ous cases of bronchial and pulmonary diseases in conse- quence of the severity oft he weather. On the 4th of the month the escape of sulphuretted hydrogen. between the hours of 5-30 and 8 p.m. was conspicuous all over the town, also on the Bth inst. On the 26th inst. it was reported to me that on the previous night the inhabitants of Farnworth were nearly suffocated with it. This was clearly traceable to the works and not to the waste heaps."—On the motion of Mr. Cook the minutes were confirmed.

LIBERAL MEETING AT EARLESTOWN.

Sir,—Will you grant me a little space to suggest to Mr. Neill' s Chairman, that he would do well to muzzle local Speakers. One of these gentlemen on Saturday night completely spoiled a splendid meeting by droning for half-an-hour, dosing the electors with political spoon- meat, seasoned with personalities, quite oblivious to one fact, that the meeting was not called to listen to him. He apparently thought such a chance might never occur again. The consequence was that there was little time left for the gentlemen who followed the candidate,whorn the electors were anxious to hear.
The best way to sit on these gentlemen is to ask them for a subscription to the funds of the Association.— Yours,
LIBERAL.

div.head: UNMERCIFUL JUSTICE.
div.p: UNMERCIFUL JUSTICE.

Sir,—Permit me through your eolumns to call the attention of all right feeling Englishmen to a miscar- riage of justice which took place in our midst the other day. A poor, but honest and struggling fellow creature —partially blind—who has maintained a wife and family some time by the making of temperance drinks. which he retailed to the employs of a forge in the neighbour- hood of Sankey Bridges was the victim. Through his in- ability to see, he wheeled a perambulator containing his thirst quenchers onto the footpath, when he was accosted by one of the law and order fraternity. nis name and address were taken, and he was subsequently summoned and fined ss. and costs, or seven days' imprisonment. Being unable to pay the fine, this poor fellow has been deprived of the means of obtaining a livelihood for his wife and family. Now, sir, I always thought justice was supposed to be tempered with mercy. Hoping that some abler pen than Milli will promptly take this matter up, and that this poor man will be released and recompensed,—l am, 'yours, &c., NEMO.

div.head: EARLESTOWN_COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: THE EARLESTOWN_COMMISSIONERS.

------ Sir.—At the last meeting of the above Board, it is reported, the Chairman delivered himself thus—" would just ask those gentlemen who are continu- ally writing to the newspapers on the question of the treatment of night-soil to tell the Commissioners how they were to dispose of the matter without spending money." To this I reply—let : That the various letters have rarely if ever, touched upon the question of night- soiL—though God knows they have ample room. They were almost entirely confined to that "three-Cornered folly," the proposed Public Hall.—The Chairman would have shown that he had thoroughly grasped the situa- tion if he had sebid : " Gentlemen, we are about to spend Lb 9,000, or tbereabouts, on an object of absolute inutility, which, lay the very nature of things, can only be an abortion. When we take the site into considera- tion, we find that the building must be a standing loss to the ratepayers, and a monument of our wasteful and egregious folly ; and to make it pay at all, we shall require to let the outer walls—and windows too !—to some enterprising advertiser. pith full permission to paste them ali over, Aow, gentlemen, to avoid being

the shaft for honest and well deserved ridicule to all time, I propose that we spend the £lO,OOO, in improving the sewage arrangements, purifying the lake, and provi- ding more effectual means for dealing with the night- soil." Sir, I contend that this would have been an approach to common sense, and would have shown a dis- position to deal with what is an absolute requirement in the parish, and enabled them to get rid of a very unsavoury "job." That question of money-spending will not be allowed to drop, and I warn those Commissioners who are push- ing on that building atrocity that they will have to answer for doubling the amount pledged to the rate- payers, to a Board whose duty and pleasure it is to curb wasteful and wicked expenditure. This they have been told before; and they don't seem to know that within the last few years a set of Commissioners were surcharged nearly £2,000 for the very same reason—namely, spend- ing more than they had pledged themselves to the rate- payers to do. Again, sir,—How was it that the letters of Messrs. Gillespie and Gooch were not made public, and were shelved into Committee ? I contend that these letters were not private property, and ought to have been read at the meeting, so that they could have been reported, and something like straightforwardness shown. But , when I read over the names of the members present. I was not astonished. To have opposed the Chairman and the gentleman who always says " ditto " to him, would have been like "bearding lions in their den." They were, through their surroundings at the time, absolute autocrats ; and whilst those two punished the offender for his audacity, the other " friends in council " would have said "ditto "with any amount of dots! Before closing my letter, and apropos of Colonel McCorquodale's retirement.froin the Board, may I sug- gest the propriety of having females as members ? They couldn't be worse, they wouldn't be as dumb as some, and an opportunity would be afforded to somel of the clique to introduce a relative as candidate—say a sister, a wife, or even a mother-in-law ! That " would ' be a consummation devoutly to be wished ;" and the danger—the imminent danger—of being mulcted in a large amount by the Local Government Board, would. I am certain, be avoided ; for the female perception of what is equitable and just would be an invaluable fac- tor at all their meetings. Anyway, I think I have shown the Chairman how he can dispose of the nightsoil, how he can meet the requirements of the parish, and how he can avoid a stupendous folly, and a ve7 big source of danger to his pocket. May he profit by it ! CLIQUE HATER. Newton, February 12th, 1892.

div.head: OWN LIFE POLICIEB.
div.p: OWN LIFE POLICIEB.

Sir,—l am pleased to find one has had the courage of his conviction ; and to stand forth to declare it, front among the large army of insurance officials, in this, and the surrounding districts. I trust the public and the cause of insurance will not suffer by the discussion of this question. Now that own life proposals, and policies on the lives of near and distant relatives, have found in Mr. Henry H. Dutton,a champion to fight their battle, I earnestly hope he will be able to lift the cloud of suspi- cion which so thickly surrounds these mysterious docu- ments. If he fails, I trust some other important official of any important office in this town, will try to sift the matter.

Mr. Dutton having conceded the very important point, that the laws, which were intended to direct, and compel obedience to, its provisions,and guide companies and societies and their officials, are simply ignored in these contracts, how then, can he explain the supposed policy on his father's life to be an ideal and complete document ? Why, sir, the simplest agent—or the aver- age washerwoman could tell you that such a policy is a spurious article, because it bears upon its face, only one name, the owner's name,his father's,therefore it belongs to his father—although he never paid a single penny and at his death, the widow claims, and Mr. Dutton may whistle for his portion if be be at variance with his mother, and in my case he would be entirely in her hands.

But, Mr. D. says I have an assurable interest in him. Granting this to him, and the office know this, and the agent waits upon him every week for his shilling. and both the office and the agent know that they receive it under false conditions, I ask him to consider the posi- tion and say if he would be wanting in judgment to pay on and on with such a false document, another. person's property, which will rank among the estate of the de- ceased, the prospect of his benefits being thus removed from his grasp. But to a more important matter, the entering of distant relations on our life policies. After Mr. D. has explained how his company, or society, will pay him his father's claim, without any plpstering up of the policy, by wills, and such like rubbish, he may then proceed to state how he would enter his own and wife's relatives, and of course an average stock would contain about ten uncles and aunts, fifteen brothers and sisters, about 32 cousins or half cousins, two grandfathers and mothers, besides father-in-law and mother-in:law and a host of others too numerous to mention. He will find ample accommodation for all the above host with men whose appetites for business will swallow the lot. As regards gigantic gambling propensities not having a firm hold in the insurance world, and my being mis- taken as to its extent, Mr. D. evidently does not take note of reports of weekly newspapers, or official organs of insurance,which record cases that have been exposed, quite against the interests of both office and officers, and which would certainly have been paid along with many others which ought not to be paid to save reputation. But some are too glaring and many are cooked. Gambl- ing in life policies is to the life institution what a cancer is to the body, with its thousand fangs, spreading its roots in every direction. For the present I will only give him a few out of the 20 reasons why I object to the use of these forms" Own Life" when making contracts to assure another person :- Ist. They form an unfair basis of competition bet- ween.the honest and the dishonest agent. . . . .

2nd. They tend to falsify both- the proposer, the agent, and the offices. 3rd. They tend to undermine the laws that govern contracts and bring them into disrep.ite. • 4th. They enable persons to be entered for far larger sums that would be permitted, if the right forms were used.—Youra respectfully, JOHN MOORFIELD. 44, Parker-st., Warrington. Feb. 9th, 1892.

div.head: UNANSWERED "QUESTION OF EVOLUTION."
div.p: THE UNANSWERED "QUESTION OF EVOLUTION."

While It would not be either right or reasonable to main- tain that nothing should be taught the very young which had not received the approving attestation of science, on the other hand It is quite certain that nothing should be taught which has been scientifically disproved and is discredited by a wide concensus of cultured opinion, as being incompatible with known facts. —A text from the context.

Sir,—The above extract contains the question which Mr. Butler "knows better than to give himself away" by discussing. The question as to whether it be right to teach the young what is now demonstrably untrue is one which demands, if our boasted love of truth be not the merest sham, instant investigation, and the error, if substantiated, removed. I am, indeed, sorry that the slight abrasion of his self-love by " a pointless satire," should so far have ruffled the superficial profundity of his soul as to cause him to overlook and neglect so vital and important a subject in order to be-little one who is so immeasurably his inferior in everything "above the or- dinary correspondence of a newspaper." Mr. Butler is wroth with me in that I will not allow him to " diffuse" upon the general question of evolation. I have offered to consider with him the specific question of the origin of man as far as known facts and reasonable inference from these declare it. But no. Mr. Butler, faithful to his training, wishes to soar out of sight and hail of ad- verse facts, and to pose on the Pegasus of mere opinion.

As I have before indicated, the two hypotheses claim- ing to account for man's origin stand, as regardsproof, exactly shoulder to shoulder. In both cases the verdict is :—Not Proven. But wnen we come to enquire into the relative probability of the two accounts—the evolu- tionary hypothesis is the one which has facts to sustain it. Recent archreological and geological investigation furnish abundant material evidence as to the savagery of man's earliest traces. Upon this hear the authorities. Palceolithic man was unquestionably a true troglodyte, the caves which he is known to have inhabited being very numerous"—Geikie--" Prehistoric Europe," P. 19. "01 these the earliest to appear was what they term the " Canstadt race" which is represented by crania found in the Neanderthal, the Val d' Amo, the Pyrenees, &c. This race is characterised by the more or less extra- ordinary prominence of the superciliary ridges, and by a low, narrow, and receding forehead. In short, says M. de Quatrefages, the face and cranium of the Can- , atacit man must, as a rule, have presented a strangely savage aspect.—lbid, P. 23.—Now all this, combined with the fact that these early people were a flint imple- ment-using race, is strangely at variance with the " Mil- tonic " hypothesis which demands the sudden introduc- tion of a godlike• man, who survived to the age of metals. Here the "first man" wail contemporary with both the " Bronze" and the " Iron " Age an absurdity which only needs stating to become manifest. Now lb ave no objection to telling children fairy tales ; but have a most decided aversion to their being forcibly inculcated as truths. It is assuredly a queer way of inducing a love eo, ut cr au tt eh the e bleegai sno nb iyn gt epaocwheinrgintaheesheildinbvyeracteaiteihesigoronteo day that which must be stultified in the next. And deeply must the moral degradation be felt ny him who, as schoolmaster, has to rivet these rusty intellectual fetters on the minds of 41i9 iiunday scholars, aewl on the Monday, has to eat his words and establish ties truth. Now, here is a system which, on the face of it, Is appar- ently maintained and practised by Mr. Butler, What science lam acquainted with utterly discredits this, So I appeal to my "luminous and logical " friend to chow where the light and reason somea In such practice ?

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 13, 1892. BRIMSTOOAN AN' TRAYCLE. I PEER'S ECONOMIC BUILDING SOCIETY. (MIXED.)
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 13, 1892. BRIMSTOOAN AN' TRAYCLE. I PEER'S ECONOMIC BUILDING SOCIETY. (MIXED.)

But this again would be making a present of himself. It would be an exceedingly good commercial piece of business to buy Mr. Butler by public auction and sell him,at once,at his own estimation. While lam in the asking mood may I ask Mr. Butler how a man can be said to" retreat from a position he has never assumed? Whether his "flag of truce " might not be mistaken for the " white feather ?" If he can tell where my " one great assump- tion "rears its horrid form? And if his claim for the " spiritual origin "of man be not entitled to the name of a baseless assumption ? And finally how does the human fcetal development, with its successive passage through higher types—an egg, a larva, a reptile and a tailed mammal agree with his assumption of a" spiritual origin "of this creature which at one time could not be distinguished from the fetus of a dog or a tortoise of the same age? Here again the doctrine of probabilities steps in and declares that this uterine evolution is but the reflex of man's past comical evolution.—Yours &c., JOHN PEERS. Penketh, Feb. 1892.

The third annual meeting of the Ist Warrington Peer's Economic Building Society was held in the large room at the offices, 19, King-at., on Tuesday evening. Mr. Thomas Birchall, the president, occu- pied the chair, and was supported by several of the Directors. There was a good attendance of mem- bers. The Directors, in their report said, that they had pleasure in submitting their third annual re- port and balance sheet, from which it would be seen that the position and finances of the Society were in a prosperous condition. Fourteen ballots had been held up to now, and sums amounting to £750 had been sold by the Directors during the year,in addition to the amounts advanced on appro- priations. These sales, representing ballotted shares purchased by the Society, had yielded a very good profit, and as several balloted shares had been pur- chased during the year and not as yet been resold, a continued profit from this source might be looked for in future. Out of this year's profits the Direc- tors proposed that a bonus of is. per share be paid on all paid up shares, which would absorb .£24 Bs. 61, and that the balance amounting to .£l2 Bs. 2d.. should be carried forward to next year's account. They also stated that tenders may be submitted by members at any time for the purchase of sums of from .£lOO to .£4oo.Messrs.Birchall,Smet- hurst, Taylor and Jones, were the retiring Direc- tors, but the last named did not seek re-election. Mr. Thos. Roberts,the member's auditor,also retired, but was eligible for re-election. The President opened the proceedings by a short speech, in which he called attention to the different items in the balance sheet, and expressed the opinion that the year's working showed a very satisfactory result. He proceeded to point out the desirability of every man" becoming his own landlord," and when he considered the number of Building Societies in Warrington, and the number of members they each had, it spoke well for the thrifty working-men of the town, aud he thought that Warrington was not by any means behindhand in the number of its citizens who were anxious to become good and ree- -1 ponsible inhabitants by becoming owners of the houses they lived in. The balance sheet was then adopted. Messrs. Birchall, Smethurst and Taylor, I were re-elected Directors, and Mr. John Bradshaw was elected to the vacant position. Mr. Thomas Roberts was illso unanimously re-elected member's auditor. A hearty vote of thanks to the President brought the proceedings to a close.

div.head: CROFT.
div.p: CROFT.

TEL PARTY AND BALL.—A tea party and ball took place at the Joiners' Arms Hotel, on Saturday evening, but there was only a small attendance. The clubroom was tastefully decorated, and art excellent tea was pro- vided. Afterwards, dancing was engaged in until clos-' ing time, Messrs. L. Daintith and D. Faxackerley, of Croft, supplying the music. &mummy cis. A Bowtixo Ctun.—lt having been decided to form a bowling club, in connection with the bowling green at the Horse Shoe Inn, on Saturday even- ing, the laost and hostess, Mr. and Mts. Maines, provided a free potato pie supper for intending members. After- wards, a meeting was held, when Mr. W. F. Pennington presided. The enrolment of members was then proceeded with, the number of entries being 30, after which the election of a committee and officers took place as follows z—Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins, president ; Mr. T. Oakes, vice-president ; Mr. Isaac Maines, treasurer ; Mr. W. F. Pennington, secretary ; and Messrs. C. Allen, Joseph Daintith, T. Houghton, A. Pomfret, John Sanderson, and H. Shaw, committee of management. The evening was spent in a convivial manner. This is the Erst club of the kind which has been formed in I Graft.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

SALE OE WORIC.—The Congregational sale of work was again opened on Saturday,and a brisk business was done. A" rumble jumble" sale was held towards the close of the evening, for the purpose of disposing of the remaining goods. The amount realised is about £6O. THE CONGREGATIONAL GUILD.—The first social tea meeting of this session of the Congregational Guild of young men and women took place in the schoolroom on Tuesday evening. There was a good attendance, and after tea the evening was pleasantly spent in games and recreation.

--WES—L—EYIN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.— The usual weekly meeting of this society was held on Mon- day evening, when a paper on " Ignatius Loyola and the Jesuits" was read by Mr. Upson. Messrs. Thorpe, Allen, E. Moston, and Taylor discussed the subject, the essayist replying to their criticisms. WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—Mr. Upson read a paper before the members of this Society on Monday evening, on "Ignatius Loyola and the Jesuits." The paper was discursive and highly interest lag; Messrs. Thorp, E. Moston, Allen, and Taylor criticised, and the essayist replied. Tux LATE REV. C. H. SPURGEON.—The Rev. C. Clay preached an obituary sermon on Sunday evening in the Congregational Church, as a token of respect for the great preacher who passed away during the week. He took his text from the words, " I have kept the faith, I have finished my course," and afterwards gave an in- teresting biographical sketch of the earlier life and later works of the rev. gentleman. There was a large con- gregation present.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.
WRSLISYAN BRASS BAND.

Last evening week in connection with the Wes- ' leyan Sunday School a grand vocal and instrumental concert, in aid of the Wesleyan Brass Band, was given in the schoolroom. There was a large attend- ance, the room being crowded. Mr. T. Gandy presided. The programme, which was excellently rendered, included selections by the Warrington United Prize Band, conducted by Mr. Meredith; songs, Miss Pigot ; violin duet. Mr. R. Foster, and Mr. Woolman ; cornet solos,Mr. G. Guest ; quartette, Messrs. R Foster, Woolman, H. Scott Jones, and A. P. Garnett ; songs, Mrs. Gutley ; recitation. Mr. W. E. Ashton; song, Miss Signum ; instrumental trio, Messrs. R. Foster. H. Scott Jones, and A. P. Garnett. The Misses Moses and Pigot accompanied the various pieces on the piano in an able manner. The meet- ing was concluded by the singing of the National Anthem. MUTUAL IXPROVIOdIINT ASSOCIATION. The usual weekly meeting of the above Associa- tion was held on Wednesday evening in the school- room. There was only a moderate attendance. Mr. Peers occupied the chair.—Mr. R. Garnett, J.P., delivered a lecture on "Palestine." illustrated by limelight views. Mr. Garnett continued the lecture he gave at the commencement of the session, tak- ing up the thread of his discourse from Jerusalem; from here, on through Hebron, Bethany, Bethlehem right up north to Damascus. The manners, cus- toms, and dress of the people were all dealt with. The condition of the country, physically, al3O re- ceived attention. The whole of the lecture was rendered specially interesting by very fine limelight illustrations, many,of the photographs having been taken by Mr. Garnett himself. Mr.R.E. Garnett ably manipulated the lantern.—At the conclusion of the lecture, a hearty vote of thanks was proposed and unanimously accorded to Mr. Garnett and Mr. R. E. Garnett.

div.head: PRESBYTERIAN CONGREGATIONAL TEA
div.p: PRESBYTERIAN CONGREGATIONAL TEA
PARTY.

The annual congregational party in connection with St. John's Presbyterian Church, Warrington, was held on Wednesday evening, in the schoolroom adjoining that building. About 120 persons partook of tea, and the tables were presided over by Mes- dames Thompson, Smith, Barlow, Longdin, Haw- thorne, Henderson, Sudlow, Sherlaw, McLarty, and Miller. At the after social meeting,which was well attended, the ex-Mayor, Alderman Francomb, pre- sided, and was supported on the platform by the Rev. J. Warnock,and Messrs. Blackburne,B.Shearer, Fulton, Smith,Sherlaw, Lees,Leark, Hawthorne, and Patterson.

The CHAIRMAN, in opening the pro- ceedings, observed that there was such a friendly feeling among the congregation of that church, that it was always a pleasure to come amongst them. Referring to the Sunday school, he said he hoped the Sabbath school would always be an institution ,of this country. Unless children got the advantage of a good and useful religious training, secular training would be of very little use. Children who went to Sunday school were mostly the children of the working- classes. For some reason or other you did not see the children of richer people attending Sunday schools. lie did not know why this was, but per- haps they got more training at home by their par- ents. He thought it would be a very good thing if the poor class of children could' mix with those more favourably circumstanced. The Chairman,. refer- ring to the necessity of good teachers in Sun- day schools, said he had seen men teaching in them who could scarcely read the Bible themselves or write their names. He pointed out that good example was an essential in the training of child- ren, and instanced the case of a child thief at the Warrington police court this week as a proof of the bad results of the absence of this example. He thought if there was not so much preaching from the pulpit and there was more visiting from house to house there would be better results. Those very peculiar people called the Salvation Army, though they did not perhaps agree with his notions of religion, yet were getting hold of the outcasts of society, and he believed were doing an immense amount ot good, much more good than the men who, clothed in purple and fine linen were preaching to aristocratic congregations. (Applause. His idea of a Sunday school was tha. children coming under the influence of a well edu- cated male or female as a teacher were found to de- rive benefit. The force of example was a remarkable i thing, and t was remarkable how children imit- ated those above them. He once heard an infidel say if he only had the training of a boy for the first two years of his life he would defy the whole bishops and curates and all denominations to make that boy a Christian afterwards. This showed the necessity of bringing children under Christian influence from the first. The Rev, J. WARNOCK then addressed the meet- ing. He remarked that during the past year they had done very well, and in one or two things un- commonly well. Me referred to the removal of the organ from the gallery to the ground floor, and the repair of the heating apparatus as improvements. Upwards of .£72 had been raised by the congrega- tion for these objects. An entertainment was given, including songs by Miss Jones, who obtained an encore. Messrs. Black- burn and Longdin. cornet solos by At r. Armstrong, glees by the choir, and a recitation by Mr. Hunter. After the usual votes of thanks, the proceedings were concluded devotionally,

div.head: NEW LOCAL STEAMER.
div.p: THE NEW LOCAL STEAMER.
SUPPER TO.SHIP_YARD HANDS.

On Saturday the whole of the employes Of Messrs Smith and Co., of Lytham, concerned in the build- ing and launching of the Helvetia,which took place the week previous, were entertained to supper at the Market Hotel, Lytham, by the kindness of Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co., of Warrington, the owners of the vessel in question. Supper was served in the spacious dining-room of the hotel at seven o'clock in the evening, when the guests ' invited, to • the number of between 60 and 70, including representatives from all the numerous handicrafts employed in the building of an iron steamer, assembled round the well-spread tables. Mr. J. Ward, employed by Messrs. Monk, Hall, and Co., as superintendent at the construction of the Helvetia, presided. Mr. F. Spink, manager of Messrs Smith and Co.'s shipbuilding yard, was also present. The supper was most excellent and was fully enjoyed. Mr. F. Spink proposed a vote of thanks to Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Co.. for their kindness. The vote being carried amidst hearty cheers, Mr. J. Ward returned thanks for the firm, reading a letter received from !Air. F. W. Monks, in which the latter gentleman expressed his regret that that evening being the opening night cf the Field Club, of which he was chairman, prevented him being present at the •supper. The letter also declared the satisfaction which was felt at the manner in which Messrs. Smith and Co. had , built the Helvetia, and stated that should Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Co. require another boat, they would give that firm the preference. Mr. Ward then proposed the toast "Success to the Helvetia, her owners., her crew, and All those concerned in her construction," which wee received with enthusiasm. Mr.Spink acknowledged the compliment paid to the firm of Messrs. Smith and Co. The company then separated, having spent an exceedingly pleasant evening.

div.head: FUNERAL OF THE LATE MR, GEORGE
div.p: FUNERAL OF THE LATE MR, GEORGE
WOODS.

The funeral of the late Mr. George Woods, whose death we recorded last week, took place on Satur- day. The remains were brought by an early train from Southport, where the deceased gentleman died, to the Central Station at Warrington. The funeral eorays started from the Central Station at about a quarter past eleven. The hearse was preceded by a private carriage containing the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton and Mr. Spencer Wellhead (solicitor to the Longford Wire Co.), then came about 30 workmen of the Longford Wire Iron and Steel Company, Ltd., of which the late Mr. Wooda was a managing , director, and following the hearse were several ' carriages containing relatives and friends of the deceased, and a number of clerks from the offices. From the number cf blinds of private houses lowered, and the shutters of several shops being put up en route to the cemetery, it was very evident that the deceased was highly respected. Among those present were Mr. Edwin Woods (brother) managing director of tho Longford Co., Mr. Arthur Woods (brother), Mr. W. Woods (brother), Mr. J. Lee (brother-in-law), Master T. Woods, W. S. Woods, Stanley Wilson (cousin), and three nephews.; Mr. Charles White (deceased's medical attendant), Mr. R. Pierpoint (Conservative candidate for Werring- ton), Alderman Francomb, Alderman Wright, Councillors L. Greening, and R. Heaton, Messrs. J. L. Tunstall and J. R. Young (directors of the Longford Co.), Messrs. J. Harrison, J. A. Hind, A. Vernon, 11. S. Wellhead, J. Crank, A. Keenan, and J. O'Shea (Clerks of the Longford Company), Messrs. W. Richardson, J. Richardson, I'. Caldwell, J. P. Fraser, (Messrs. Pierpoint and Fraser), Stanley Higham (manager of tI.• Con- servative Club), T. Whittle, and J. Westgarth. The body was borne on the shoulders of the following workmen from the chapel the graveside : Messrs. T. Bennett, D. Clayton, G. Goodwin, J. Sinis- ter. F. Hall. and W. Bartley. The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton officiated at the cemetery. A number of beautiful wreaths had been receiv.d from the widow of the deceased, and from the following relatives, friends, and employes :—Mr. and Mrs. Edwin Woods, Mr. and Mts. Joseph Lee, Mrs. 14m. Woods, Mr. and Mrs. Alfred. Woods, Misses Woods, Mrs. Wilson, Mr. and Mrs. W. S. Woods, Mr. and Mrs. W. H. Har- rison, Clerks of the Longford Co., employes, Mr. and Mrs. J. L. Tunstall, Mr. and Mrs. Thomas Tun- stall, Mr. and Mrs. J. J. Thompson, (Sale), Mr. Chas. Peace, (Sheffield), Mr. and Mrs. J. R. Young, Mr. and Mrs. J. Westgarth, !Warrington Conservative Club, Mr. and Mrs. Thomas Whittle, Mr. and ]kErs. R. H. Pearson, Messrs. W. :and J. Richardson, Mr. Oliver, (Liverpool).

div.head: WARRINGTON ANGLERS ASSOCIATION.
div.p: WARRINGTON ANGLERS ASSOCIATION.
LECTURE LAST NIGHT.

Last night in connection with the Northern Anglers Association, Warrington Centre, a lecture was delivered by the Rev. C. P. Roberts, vicar of St. John's, Longvight, vice-president of the Associa- tion, in the Masonic Hall,Sankey-street, his subject being "Reminiscencesof Loch Awe, among the perch trout pike, and salmon." Councillor H. Roberts presided, and on the platform with him was Mr. Mawson. secretary of the district council of the Association. There was a large audience which included the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton and Councillor J. H. Fleming, and several ladies. Prior to the commencement of the proceedings, Mr. Galloway entertained those present with some excellent performances on the organ. The Chairman explained the objects of the association, and said the object of having a lecture was to let it be known that the association was in existence, and to obtain additional members. Those who lived in towns like Warrington knew only too well the difficulties there were in the way of fisher- men procuring anything like decent sport. In the waters in the immediate neighbourhood it was I either absolutely prohibited to the general body of anglerA, or they were so difficult of access,that very few people indeed could get to them. One of the objects of the association was to get further pro- tection for the public in waters in which there was now free fishing, and he thought that onght to be sufficient to induce all anglers to join it. The Rev. C. P. ROBERTS then gave an interesting and chatty account of his experiences in fishing in Loch Awe for perch, trout, pike, and salmon. He described the habits and characteristics of these fish and the methods he had found most available for catching them. The perch, he said, was a slug- gish greedy fellow, and seemed to take all that was put before him, and it did not very much matter as to the quality or quantity. It did not want slily approaching like the trout. In the gale that destroyed the Tay Bridge the perch in the Loch Leven were washed ashore by tone. The perch could not battle against winds and waves, whilst the trout was a pretty nimble fellow and could take care of himself. The pike had been introduced into Loch Awe by the Marquis of Breadalbane, the first one caught startling the fisherman who drew it out, and now the natives were trying to exter- minate the pike in the Loch, 3d. or 6d. per fish being I paid for their capture. The lecturer in detailing his salmon fishing experiences said it was curious that nothing was ever found in the salmon's stomach. It had either very quick digestion or could discharge the contents of its stomach on being hooked.—The usual votes of thanks were accorded.

A general strike under the auspices of the Coal Por- ters' Union was commenced in London on Wednesday, about 10,000 men being affected. By the explosion of a locomotive at Philadelphia, three railway servants have been killed and four seriously in- jured. A Barcelona telegram of Wednesday states that on the previous evening a bomb was exploded in the heart of the town, killing three persons and severely injuring three others.
On Thursdiy morning Mr. Freake, son of Sir T. Freake, whilst hunting with the Cricklades Hounds near Swindon, was thrown from his horse and dislocated his neck, dying instantly.
The Board of Agriculture, in consequence of the dis- covery of foot-and-mouth disease, has issued further orders prohibiting all importations of cattle from the Netherlands.

.„ The writ for the Everton election was issued in the House of Commons on Wednesday, on the motion of Mr. Akers-Douglas, and the nomination will take place ow Monday and the polling on Wednesday. smovisTo ConcaT.—On Saturday evening a smoking . concert took place the Golborne Conservative Club, under favourable circumstances. There was a good at- tendane, over which Mr. W. H. Arnofi, J.P., C.C., of Lowton, presided.
The directors of Brunner, Mond, and Co.,alkali manu- facturers, in their report, recommend a divi- dend of 50 per cent, on the ordinary shares for the past half-year.
CHILD KILLED BY A LAMP EXPLOSION.
A lamp exploded at Birkenhead, yesterday, killing a child aged three, who was sitting on its father's knee. 'file father also was seriously injured.

THE COAL STRIKE. A conference between union representatives of the men on strike and members of the Coal Merchants Association held at the London Coal Exchange yesterday afternoon was without definite result.
CFIARGE OF ATTEMPTED MURDER AND SUICIDE.

At Rochester, yesterday, a man named Corbett was remanded, charged with attempting to murder Elizabeth Edwards, and with attempting suicide at Northfleet, on Sunday. The parties, who were lovers, were found with their throats cut, and both had razors in their possession. Miss Edwards' condition is critical.

div.head: RESOLUTION TO STOP THE COLLIERIES.
div.p: RESOLUTION TO STOP THE COLLIERIES.

Yesterday at a conference of the National Miners' Federation, at Manchester, a resolution was carried in favour of the stoppage of the collieries, a further confe- rence to be held the first week of the stoppage, to con- sider the question of further stoppage. It was also re- solved that notices be handed in to expire on March 12th.

SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A MOTHER. At Harlesden, yesterday, Emily Saville, 24, married woman, was committed for trial charged with attempt- ing to poison herself and her three children with laud- anum. The evidence showed that the accused and her husband were extremely poor, and she had remarked to her sister, "If the childrne and I were not here, he could pay his debts."

div.head: TRIAL OF MRS. OSBORNE.
div.p: THE TRIAL OF MRS. OSBORNE.

Mrs. Osborne was again brought up at Bow-street., yesterday, on the charge of having committed perjury in her evidence as plaintiff in the celebrated Pearl case. A large crowd assembled at the entrance to the court, but the accommodation being of a limited character,very few were admitted. The accused was calm of demean- our, but wept copiously. Captain Osborne again took up a position by the dock, and Major and Mrs. Har- greave were present, accompanied by their solicitor. Mr. Spink was next called, and repeated his evidence as to the purchase, on Febrhary 19th, of the jewels from the accused, to her giving and signing the name " A. Price "and to her return, on the 23rd, to get the cheques cashed. Mr. Gill here said he proposed to ask for a committal for perjury and larceny. Mr. Pearce, cashier at Glyn's Bank, deposed to cashing the cheque for the accused on February 23rd. He was certain about her identity. Mr. Cortham, ac- countant at the Piccadily branch of the National Pro- vincial Bank, deposed to a lady changing £550 from gold to notes at that establishment on February 23rd. Mr. Gill said the notes had been traced.
Mrs. Osborne, who had nothing to say. was com- mitted on the double charge, and removed to Hollo- way.

div.head: YESTERD,VY'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: YESTERD,VY'S PARLIAMENT.
THE SHIP CANAL
WAGES, &c.

Another batch of men employed on the canal at Thel- wall have been dismissed from the Canal Company's em- ploy. It was proposed to reduce the watchmen's wages, but the men strongly objected, and gained their point.

FAT A LITY AT NORTON. Mr.J. E. Worsley, the coroner, on Tuesday, held an inquest at the L. and N. W. Hotel,Runcorn,on the body of George Chalmers, a labourer 62 years of age. The deceased was employed on the Ship Canal works at Big Field and on the morning of the 29th January he travelled by the " Mail" train to his work. After alighting from the train he walked along the line and hearing a train of waggons coming he crossed on to another set of metals when an engine coming in the contrary iirection knocked him down and went over him. Hi-escaped the wheels but the breakguards crushed him. A young man named Joseph Powell assisted him to rise and to get on the engine and he said he would be taken to his lodge in Spring-st., Runcorn, in preference to the hospital. He stood on the engine during the journey, and although he complained of pains in the hips and body he did not appear to think himself very bad. he was attended by Dr. Mc Dou- gall up to the time of his death on Monday. He had described how the accident occured to his landlady Mrs. Fanny Wood. and he had said that after the engine was stopped it was backed over him again, but the driver and other witnesses showed that this was not correct. The driver Thomas Reeves stated that the morning was very dark and his engine was fully provided with lamps. He also whistled at that point where the accident occured. A verdict of accidental death was recorded,

div.head: DEEP DOCK FOR RUNCORN.
div.p: DEEP DOCK FOR RUNCORN.

On Thursday a depulation from the Runcorn Board of Improvement Commissioners waited upon the Commit- tee of the Manchester Ship Canal Co., with reference to the provision of deep dock at Runcorn, to accommodate vessels of deep draught. Tha deputation consisted of Messrs. H. J. Grice, (chairman), J. W. Lightburn, Jas. Pritchards, S. Taylor, and P. Speakman C.C. The com- mittee was presided over by Mr. Bithell, and a represen- tative of the Manchester Corporation was present. Ths interview occupied half-an-hour, and the impression conveyed to the deputation was that the Company would endeavour to meet the wishes of the Commissioners in the matter, and would communicate definitely as soon as possible.
A COUNTY COURT PRISONER ESCAPES FROM CONFINEMENT.

On Wednesday afternoon, Wm. Percival, potato and commission merchant, of Hill Cliff, against whom there had been for some time a County Court warrant for commitment for non-payment of a debt of .El9,was apprehended in the Warrington Market, and he was immediately lodged in the police cells. At nine o'clock on Thursday morning,he was, purely as a matter of consideration for his comfort, re- moved to the County Court, and there locked up in a large room in the top storey of the building pend- ing conveyance to prison. Some two hours later the prisoner's brother called with the object of making some arrangement as to the payment of the debt,and he, accompanied by the bailiff, proceeded upstairs to interview the debtor. To their astonish- ment the door of the room in which he had been immured was found open, the bailiff, as may be imagined, giving utterance to an exclamation ex- pressive of supreme mortification and surprise. The prisoner had unscrewed the lock of the door, opened it, and came down two flights of stairs, had passed the entrance to the court room in which cases were being heard at the time, and the high bailiff's .ofilee and had made his exit by the front door and got clear away. He has since been heard in a public- house at Stockton Heath to boast of his achieve- ment, but, though by latest accounts he had not been re-captured, there is no doubt, that his brother not having been able to accomodate matters for him, his triumph will be but short-lived.

HOUSE OF LORDS. The House of Lords met at quarter past four. Lord MIDDLETON asked whether the Government were prepared to issue a Royal Commission, to inquire into the question of fogs in London, and whether they were preventable. The Marquis of Salisbury replied that an Universal use of anthracite coal would be an effective remedy. He recommended the noble Lord to move the appointment of a Committee. The House adjourned five minutes past five. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. MISCELLLANEOUS.—CoIoneI BaoonrlELD gave notice of a Bill to prohibit the use of hop substitutes in the brew- ing of beer. The Secretary for War denied that one undue proportion of work was being given out to Gov- ernment factories at the expense of private firms. Mr. Jesse Collings brought in a Bill for giving facilities for the creation of small holdings of land. THE ADDRESS. Dr. FITZGERALD continued the debate on the amend- ment to the Address in favour of reconsideration of cases of Irish political prisoners. Sir W. HARCOURT said he had attended carefully to the debate but failed to find any new ground which would justify him in supporting the amendment. Mr. Justice McCarthy said tne Fen- ians were wild and possibly foolish revolutionaries, but outrages formed no part whatever in their programme. The debate was continued by Mr. MAHONY, Mr. ROBY, Mr. Ditt,on and others. Mn. REDMOND'S amendment was ultimately rejected by a majority of 71.
